levels.title: Underwriting judgement, file discipline and defensible recommendations

units.title: Reading the file the way underwriting reads it

lessons.title: Reading a full merchant file: the claim ledger and what silence hides
lessons.explanation: A merchant file is not a story and not a sales checklist. It is a claim ledger: a set of assertions about revenue, tenure, ownership, obligations and behaviour, each of which carries a source, a date and a method. Underwriting work begins when you write the assertions down in one column and, in the next, the evidence that supports each one. The standard inventory for a small-business funding file includes the signed application and any statutorily required disclosures; bank and card processor statements for a defined window; the processor's own settlement reports; business tax returns or transcripts; an interim profit and loss statement; a debt schedule naming every obligation, its payment, its frequency and its remaining balance; a UCC search result; a lien and judgment search; the lease or property documents; ownership and control documents; every prior agreement for financing still outstanding, with payoff figures; identity and ownership verification for the owners who will sign; and the personal financial statement of any guarantor. The discipline is simple to state and hard to hold: an assertion with a source of the merchant's own making is weaker than an assertion from an independent record, and an assertion with no source at all is not evidence of anything. That last category is where most of the analytical value sits, because absent items are not neutral. Four months of statements missing from twelve is not four months of zero revenue; it is four months of unknown revenue, and unknown revenue is priced into whatever recommendation follows. Silence has a shape. A merchant who supplies three months when twelve were requested may be showing a deteriorating trend, or a three-month spike that would look thin against the year. A file with no UCC search has no defensible statement about lien priority. A file with no lease has no answer to occupancy. A file with a verbal reference to a prior advance and no payoff letter has no basis for a stacking conclusion. The right first move is rarely a decline and rarely a sale; it is a verification plan that names what is missing, who can produce it, how long it takes, and what the file would support at each stage.
lessons.example: Rosewood Cafe submits a fourteen-item file. Nine items are documented: application, three months of processor settlements, four months of bank statements, a signed personal financial statement, an identification document, a lease, an internal profit and loss statement, and a debt schedule naming one equipment loan. Five are not: eight of the twelve months of bank statements, the business tax return, a UCC search, a payoff letter for a prior advance that the merchant mentioned in conversation, and any document establishing the ownership percentages of two silent partners. The completeness ratio is nine of fourteen, which is 64.29 percent. The merchant's written claim of prior-year revenue is $412,000. The four months of statements actually provided sum to $106,300 on the merchant's own seasonal pattern, and the merchant's summary shows the year at $318,400 in deposits, so the claim exceeds the deposited evidence by $93,600, or 22.72 percent of the claim. The missing four months are, by the merchant's own summary sheet, the four strongest months of the year. None of this proves misstatement; processor settlements can trail bank deposits, cash receipts can be deposited late, and a summary sheet can be wrong in either direction. What it does do is convert a vague discomfort into four named questions with named sources. The underwriter's written position becomes: the file as submitted supports an advance sized on $318,400 of deposited revenue, not $412,000; the file cannot support any priority statement until the UCC search is run; and no guarantee schedule can be finalised until ownership is documented, because the people who sign depend on who owns.
lessons.question: A merchant says a prior advance was already paid off and offers to email a screenshot of a zero balance. What does a defensible file record require, and why is the screenshot not the answer?
lessons.answer: A payoff letter or statement from the prior funder, dated, on the funder's own record, and a fresh UCC search showing whether the financing statement has been terminated or assigned. The screenshot is a merchant-generated image with no verifiable source and can show a servicing screen without showing whether the lien was released.
lessons.distractor: The screenshot is sufficient because a zero balance and a paid-off account mean the obligation and any related lien end at the same moment.
lessons.correction: Balance and lien are separate facts. A paid-off advance can leave a financing statement of record, and priority questions turn on the filing record, not on the merchant's balance screen. The file needs a document from the funder and a search result, both dated, because the analysis depends on who holds a perfected interest on the day of closing.

depth.definitions: A claim ledger is the one-page pairing of every material assertion with its evidence source and date. Provenance is the origin of a document: an independent record such as a bank statement or processor report, a merchant-generated record such as a summary sheet or profit and loss statement, or a merchant assertion with no record at all. Corroboration means two sources that can be checked against each other, for example processor settlements against bank deposits. A negative confirmation is evidence that a check was run and produced nothing, such as a UCC search returning no financing statement naming the debtor, and it is evidence in its own right. A completeness ratio is the count of documented items divided by the count of items the file standard requires, expressed as a percentage; it is a management device, not a credit score and not a reason for a decision on its own. A condition is a requirement that must be satisfied before funding; a decline is a decision not to fund. The two are different answers to the same file and should never be blurred in a conversation.
depth.mechanism: Underwriting discounts evidence by distance from the source. An independent third-party record that the merchant cannot edit sits at the top; a merchant-generated record that can be reconciled to an independent record sits in the middle; a merchant assertion with no record sits at the bottom and is usable only for questions, never for conclusions. This hierarchy explains why the same number can be acceptable in one file and not in another: a $40,000 monthly deposit figure reconciled to twelve months of statements is a fact, while the same figure written on a form is a lead. Absent items are handled in one of three ways, and naming which one applies is the analytical move. They are verified, which costs time and may change the recommendation; they are bounded, meaning the recommendation is sized to the evidence actually present; or they are conditioned, meaning funding waits on delivery. Each has a cost the merchant should hear in plain language, including the cost of delay when a seasonal window is closing. A fourth option, ignoring the gap and hoping, is what regulators and courts later describe as failing to notice what the file said.
depth.secondExample: Consider a landscape contractor with a full twelve months of statements, a clean UCC search and documented ownership, but a structural gap of a different kind: ninety-four percent of receipts arrive through a single municipal customer, and the contract that produces them is one year into a three-year term with a renewal option the city holds. Nothing is missing here in the document sense. The merchant has supplied more than the inventory requires. The gap is analytical rather than documentary, and it changes the shape of the recommendation: the file supports a shorter obligation with a lower remittance share, or a reserve, because the concentration and the renewal option are conditions on the same cash flow that repays the advance. Contrast a second contractor in the same trade whose receipts come from forty residential clients, with two months of statements missing. That file is thinner in documents and more durable in cash flow. Reading a file means holding both dimensions at once instead of scoring one and assuming the other.
depth.mistake: The commonest error is treating a conversation as documentation. The phrase I spoke to the owner and he confirmed it belongs in a notes field, not in the evidence column, and the correction is mechanical: ask what record would exist if the statement were true, then request that record. A second error is auditing only what was submitted, so a file that arrives complete-looking is treated as complete; the fix is to work from the standard inventory and mark each line as received, received and reconciled, or absent. A third error is answering a gap with a smaller number without saying so, which leaves the merchant believing the original request is still moving; the correction is to state the sized recommendation, the verified basis for it, and the specific documents that would change it. A fourth error is running a search and not reading it, so a filed financing statement that names the owner personally rather than the company is missed. Read the debtor name field character by character against the legal name in the ownership documents.
depth.application: Optional task: build a fourteen-row file index for a fictional merchant, mark each row received, reconciled or absent, compute the completeness ratio, and write a three-sentence position. Model response: 'Nine of fourteen items are documented, a completeness ratio of 64.29 percent. The revenue claim of $412,000 is $93,600 above the $318,400 shown by the statements provided, so the file as submitted supports an advance sized on the deposited figure. Before any guarantee schedule is set, please send the business tax return, the four missing statement months, the payoff letter for the prior advance, and the ownership documents for the two partners; I have requested the UCC search and will share the result the day it arrives.' Self-review rubric: every number traceable to a named document; each gap paired with a source that could close it; the sized recommendation stated explicitly rather than implied; no approval, rate or outcome promised; no suggestion that a missing item can be skipped.
depth.summary: A file is a ledger of claims and evidence, and its gaps carry as much information as its contents. The transferable skill is the pairing habit: state the claim, name the record that would support it, judge how independent that record is, and decide whether the gap is verified, bounded or conditioned. The same habit governs buying a business, preparing a loan application, or responding to an insurer's questions, because in each case the decision-maker is reasoning about what is known, what is verified and what remains unknown.

visual.title: Claim ledger to verification plan
visual.description: A two-column layout that turns a pile of documents into a decision. The left column lists assertions a merchant has made; the right column holds the record that would support each one and a status. Rows with a status of absent feed a verification plan rather than a conclusion.
steps: Left column, in the merchant's own words: revenue last year; months in business; who owns what; every obligation and its payment; whether any prior advance exists.

Right column, the record that proves it: bank or processor statements; formation and ownership documents; a debt schedule reconciled to debits seen in bank data; a payoff letter from the prior funder.
Status each row: received, received and reconciled, or absent. Mark the absent rows in a third colour so they cannot be mistaken for zero.
Forecast value: for each absent row, name the lowest and highest number it could plausibly hold and note how the recommendation would change at each end.
Verification plan: owner, document, date promised, and the sized recommendation the file supports today versus after the item arrives.

lessons.title: Deposits as evidence: what bank and processor data actually show an underwriter
lessons.explanation: Deposits are cash arriving in an account. They are not revenue, and treating them as revenue is the single most common analytical error in small-business funding. An experienced reader works through a defined sequence. First, identify the account and the window: whose account, which months, which days, and whether the statements are complete pages rather than selected images. Second, separate operating receipts from everything else. Round-number transfers from the owner's personal account, proceeds of a loan or advance, refunds, insurance payments, transfers between the merchant's own accounts, and tax refunds all inflate gross deposits without being revenue. Third, look at the rhythm: deposits that arrive in a few large lumps behave differently from daily card settlements, and the repayment structure has to match whichever pattern is real. Fourth, test quality. Returned items, insufficient-funds notices, negative collected balances and days ending below zero describe how the account is managed, not what the business earns, and they predict how a new debit will behave. Fifth, deduct obligations already being debited. Every existing payment that hits the same account competes with the proposed remittance, and the schedule of those payments, not just their amount, tells you which weeks are tight. Sixth, compute the ratios that matter: the proposed remittance as a share of normalized deposits, combined debt service as a share of normalized deposits and of gross margin, and the count of days in which the balance fell below the proposed debit. Seventh, ask what the data cannot show. Deposits cannot tell you whether a customer paid an invoice for work delivered six weeks ago, whether revenue is billed but uncollected, or whether the merchant funds part of the business from cash. Each of those needs a different record, and naming that record is part of reading the data honestly.
lessons.example: Northgate Auto Body supplies twelve weeks of business checking statements with matching processor reports. Gross deposits for the window are $284,600. Working through the credits line by line, the reader removes $18,000 of transfers from the owner's personal account, $25,000 of proceeds from an equipment loan deposited in week two, and $12,400 moved in from a second account the same owner controls, including a round $6,000 pair three days apart. Normalized operating deposits are $284,600 less $55,400, which is $229,200, or $19,100 a week. Existing obligations debited to the same account are $2,750 a week, equal to $33,000 across the window, leaving $196,200, or $16,350 a week, before any new obligation. A proposed remittance of $1,600 a week is 8.38 percent of normalized deposits, and total debt service of $4,350 a week is 22.77 percent. The statements also show seven insufficient-funds or returned-item notices and eleven days closing with a negative collected balance out of eighty-four calendar days, which is 13.10 percent of days. The merchant's own summary describes the period as consistent and strong. The defensible reading is narrower: receipts are steady when the transfers are stripped out, the account is run close to zero roughly one day in eight, and the new $1,600 debit will land on the same dates as the existing $2,750. The recommendation that follows is not necessarily no; it is a remittance sized against normalized, not gross, deposits, with the returned items explained and a plan for the weeks the debits coincide with the merchant's slowest payment cycle.
lessons.question: A merchant's account shows $510,000 of deposits in six months, including two $30,000 transfers from the owner's savings and a $45,000 deposit from a new lender. The merchant wants an advance sized on revenue of about $1 million a year. What is the first correction?
lessons.answer: Strip the non-operating credits: the owner transfers and lender proceeds are not revenue, and the remaining operating deposits are the basis for sizing. State the corrected figure, the arithmetic behind it, and what would change it.
lessons.distractor: Average the deposits and note that the two transfers are self-funding, because money moved from the owner's savings is money the owner could contribute again if the business falters.
lessons.correction: A past transfer is not a commitment, and counting it as revenue both overstates the business and understates the risk. The correction is arithmetic first: deposits less transfers, loan proceeds, refunds and inter-account movements. Then ask what the corrected figure covers, and remember that deposits include collections of work billed in earlier periods, so they lag the activity that produced them.

depth.definitions: Gross deposits are all credits to the account in the window. Normalized operating deposits are gross deposits less credits that are not receipts from customers: owner contributions and personal transfers, loan or advance proceeds, refunds, insurance recoveries, tax refunds and transfers between related accounts. Gross margin here means revenue less the variable cost of delivering it, expressed in dollars and as a percentage. Combined debt service is existing periodic obligations plus the proposed new payment. Coverage is gross margin divided by combined obligations plus fixed operating cost, and it is an illustrative test rather than a rule. Negative days are days ending with a below-zero collected balance. A return is a credit reversed and sent back, often because the depositing party lacked funds. A remote deposit capture or lockbox arrangement is a structure in which receipts are collected and applied under the funder's or bank's control rather than the merchant's.
depth.mechanism: Deposits live in an account that has a rhythm and a queue. The queue matters as much as the rhythm, because obligations are met on dates, not averages. Two merchants with identical weekly deposits can have completely different experiences: one has the existing debits on the third and seventeenth, the other on the same two days as the proposed remittance, so the second one doubles the depth of the trough twice a month. That is why underwriting reads the debit calendar beside the deposit pattern, and why a share-of-receipts structure is a design answer to a lumpy queue rather than a marketing preference. Returned items and negative days are read as behaviour under stress: they show where the margin between inflow and outflow sits in practice, not just on a spreadsheet, and a merchant who has run with a five-hundred-dollar buffer for a year will feel a new debit differently from one who has held three weeks of expenses. The reading is deliberately conservative because a funding obligation is a fixed claim and the data is being used to decide whether a fixed claim can tolerate a variable month.
depth.secondExample: Take a freight broker whose deposits are healthy in total but arrive from a small number of large clients on sixty-day terms. Weekly deposits average $24,000, but the standard deviation is wide: four weeks in the sample land under $9,000 and two land above $52,000. A $2,400 weekly remittance is ten percent of the average and would be twenty-seven percent of the four weakest weeks, which is where a debit-driven structure fails. Now compare a restaurant with the same $24,000 weekly average arriving as card settlements every business day, none below $3,100. The same $2,400 remittance is eight percent on the average and thirteen percent even in the weakest week. Same headline number, opposite structural verdict. The broker can tolerate a remittance tied to collections, a larger reserve, or a payment date after the heaviest collection week; the restaurant can carry a daily or weekly debit. The mechanism is not that one business is better, but that the funding instrument has to match the shape of the inflow.
depth.mistake: The recurring error is using gross deposits as revenue and then computing affordability against that inflated base, which makes an unaffordable obligation look comfortable. The diagnosis is asking which credits are customer receipts and having the merchant mark them; the correction is to publish the normalized figure in writing and size against it. A second error is reading only the aggregate and missing a single large irregular deposit that the merchant describes as a one-off, then discovering it was the prerequisite to the whole repayment plan. A third error is treating returned items as a character issue and moving on, when they are a mechanism issue: they show how little slack exists and how the account behaves when a debit lands early because of a weekend or holiday. A fourth error is assuming the account you can see is the only account the business uses, which understates performance; ask directly for every account and processor the business uses, because a missing account can be either a hidden strength or a hidden obligation.
depth.application: Optional task: normalize a fictional twelve-week deposit series by removing non-operating credits, then compute weekly normalized deposits, the proposed remittance as a percentage, combined debt service as a percentage, and the number of days below the proposed debit. Model response: 'Gross deposits of $284,600 include $55,400 of non-operating credits, so normalized operating deposits are $229,200, or $19,100 a week. Existing debits of $2,750 a week and a proposed $1,600 a week together are $4,350, which is 22.77 percent of normalized deposits. There are eleven negative days and seven returned items; please explain each returned item and confirm the dates your two existing debits hit, because they arrive in the same week as the new one and I want to see whether the balance holds in your slowest week.' Self-review: the correction arithmetic shown openly; no annualised rate invented; existing obligations listed with dates; the merchant's own summary distinguished from the verified record; no promise that the structure will be approved.
depth.summary: Deposits describe cash movement; normalization turns them into a usable view of the business, and the queue turns them into a usable view of repayment. The transferable method is to separate what arrived from what was earned, to test the account's behaviour under stress, to place the new obligation on the same calendar as the existing ones, and to say plainly what the data cannot show. The same reading applies to reviewing a co-borrower's account, auditing a subscription business's churn-affected receipts, or checking a contractor's progress-billing pattern before extending terms.

visual.title: From gross deposits to a repayable figure
visual.description: A waterfall that subtracts non-operating credits from gross deposits, then places existing and proposed obligations on the same weekly calendar so the shape of the trough is visible.
steps: Bar one: gross deposits for the window, with the statement months labelled.
Subtract and label each non-operating credit: owner transfers, loan or advance proceeds, related-account movements, refunds and recoveries. The remainder is normalized operating deposits.
Convert the remainder to a weekly figure and mark the range, not only the average, so the weakest weeks are visible.
Place every existing periodic obligation on the calendar, then the proposed remittance, and mark the days where both fall in the same week.
Add the quality row beneath the timeline: returned items, negative days, and any week where the balance would have gone below zero with the new debit included.

lessons.title: Seasonality: normalizing the year and matching the payment cadence
lessons.explanation: Annual revenue hides shape, and shape decides whether a payment schedule can be met. Seasonal analysis has four steps. First, put receipts in the period the industry actually lives in, which is often a week or a month rather than a quarter. Second, identify the peak and the trough and compute their ratio. A business whose weakest month is a little over half its strongest has a different tolerance from one whose weakest is a third. Third, count the periods in which a proposed fixed obligation would exceed a stated share of that period's receipts, because the number of tight periods matters more than the depth of any single one: six difficult periods a year is a chronic condition, one is a timing problem. Fourth, decide what structure fits. Options include a fixed debit that is small enough for the trough, a fixed debit with a scheduled pause in the low season, a percentage-of-receipts structure that rises and falls with collections, and a percentage structure with a fixed preset amount that is reconciled afterwards against actual receipts. That last design appears in statute in some states: Virginia defines sales-based financing to include both a repayment that moves with sales or revenue and a fixed payment with a true-up mechanism that reconciles the amount to a percentage of sales or revenue. Under any of these designs, the reconciliation is not a courtesy. It is the mechanism that makes the structure honest, and the file should state who performs it, how often, from which records, and what happens when the merchant's receipts come in below the preset amount for two periods in a row. Maturity should point the same way as the season: a facility whose term ends in the merchant's trough forces a renewal or a balloon at the worst moment, which is a design failure rather than bad luck.
lessons.example: Harborline Marine Supply provides twelve months of receipts: $41,000 in January, $38,000 in February, $46,500 in March, $52,000 in April, $61,000 in May, $68,000 in June, $72,000 in July, $66,500 in August, $58,000 in September, $49,000 in October, $44,500 in November and $61,000 in December, totalling $657,500 and averaging $54,791.67 a month. The trough is February at $38,000 and the peak is July at $72,000, a trough-to-peak ratio of 0.53. A fixed schedule of $5,600 a week is $24,266.67 a month. That obligation is 63.86 percent of February's receipts and 33.70 percent of July's. Counting the periods where it exceeds 45 percent of receipts gives six months: January, February, March, April, October and November. Six of twelve is a structural mismatch, not a soft month. Now compare a share-of-receipts structure at twelve percent: February collects $4,560 and July collects $8,640, the same percentage in both, and the merchant's obligation falls precisely when their receipts do. If the merchant prefers certainty and the funder requires a preset debit, then the honest version starts from the trough rather than the average: a preset amount sized to about thirty percent of the weakest month is $11,400 a month, which is $2,630.77 a week, with a reconciliation that refunds or credits the difference when actual receipts exceed the preset percentage, and a documented process for identifying that this has happened. The file should also record that the term is set so that the final payment does not fall in February or November.
lessons.question: A merchant's yearly revenue comfortably supports a proposed weekly remittance on an annual-average basis, and you can see that the two weakest months fall well below it. The merchant says the strong months make up for the weak months. What is the correct analysis?
lessons.answer: Count the periods in which the obligation exceeds a stated share of that period's receipts and decide whether the schedule matches the trough. Balancing across a year is not available to a fixed debit, because a payment due in February cannot be paid out of July's receipts.
lessons.distractor: Accept the annual-average argument and note the strong months as a compensating factor, since the obligation falls due monthly and the year's total is what ultimately repays it.
lessons.correction: The obligation is paid on dates and the receipts arrive in a season, so the test is per period, not per year. The correction is to size the fixed debit against the trough, shorten the schedule, add a scheduled pause, or move to a percentage-of-receipts design with a reconciliation that is defined in the agreement and actually performed.

depth.definitions: Seasonality is the recurring within-year pattern of receipts, distinguishable from a trend, which is the direction of change across years, and from noise, which is period-to-period variation without pattern. The trough-to-peak ratio is the weakest period divided by the strongest. A share-of-receipts structure collects a stated percentage of receipts, so the dollar amount varies with performance. A preset with true-up is a fixed periodic payment plus a reconciliation that adjusts the amount to the agreed percentage using verifiable records. A scheduled pause or forbearance period is a defined window in which payments are reduced or suspended by agreement. Advance and remittance have distinct meanings: the advance is the amount provided, and the remittance is what is collected and when. A factor is a multiplier applied to the advance to determine the total repayment amount, not an interest rate and not an annual percentage rate.
depth.mechanism: Two forces make seasonality bite. The first is queuing: obligations are met on dates, so a fixed debit consumes the receipts available in that week, which is why the count of tight periods rather than their depth drives the verdict. The second is the reconciliation gap. When a funder markets a percentage structure but charges a preset amount, the merchant's protection lives entirely in the true-up, and the true-up depends on records the merchant may not have produced and on a process the funder may not run. A file that names the true-up but not its mechanics is asserting a protection it cannot demonstrate, and the FTC's staff perspective notes that some providers have been observed failing to perform promised true-ups and reconciliations. The practical answer is to write the mechanics into the recommendation: which record shows actual receipts, within how many days after the period, who computes the adjustment, how the credit is delivered, and what the merchant can do if two consecutive periods pass with no adjustment. If those questions cannot be answered, the structure is a fixed debit wearing a percentage label, and it should be priced and sized as one.
depth.secondExample: An ice cream manufacturer and a snow removal contractor both have $600,000 of annual receipts and both apply in the same month. The manufacturer's peak is June through August and its trough is January at $19,000; the contractor's peak is January and February and its trough is June at $21,000. A funder that sizes both on annual averages produces the same recommendation for two opposite cash patterns, and both recommendations fail in different months. Reading the season correctly produces different designs: for the manufacturer, a percentage structure that collects more in summer and less in winter, with the term ending after the following summer, so the final collections land in a strong period; for the contractor, the mirror image, with a scheduled lighter period in June and a term that ends after the winter peak. The lesson is that the same arithmetic tool produces different answers once the calendar is included, and that a funder who cannot say which month is the trough for a specific merchant has not read the file.
depth.mistake: The classic error is comparing a periodic obligation with average revenue and declaring the structure affordable; the diagnostic question is what the obligation equals in the weakest month, and the fix is to publish that percentage every time. A second error is confusing a percentage-of-receipts promise with a percentage-of-receipts contract: if the agreement fixes a preset daily amount and the reconciliation is discretionary or undocumented, the merchant carries the seasonal risk anyway. A third error is setting a term that ends in the trough, which produces a renewal or a balloon in the merchant's weakest month and makes the merchant's difficulty a design outcome. A fourth is assuming that seasonality is stable across years; a single warm winter can flatten a contractor's peak, so the recommendation should state how many seasons the pattern has been observed and what happens if the pattern does not repeat.
depth.application: Optional task: take twelve fictional monthly receipt figures, compute the total, the average, the trough-to-peak ratio, and the percentage of receipts that a stated fixed monthly obligation consumes in each month. Model response: 'Receipts total $657,500, or $54,791.67 a month at the average, but the average conceals the shape: February is $38,000 and July is $72,000, a trough-to-peak ratio of 0.53. A fixed $5,600 weekly schedule is $24,266.67 a month, which is 63.86 percent of February and 33.70 percent of July, and it exceeds 45 percent of receipts in six of twelve months. I would rather see the schedule sized near $2,630.77 a week, which is thirty percent of February's receipts, with a documented true-up, or a twelve percent share-of-receipts design, and a term that ends outside your weak season.' Self-review: percentages computed per period rather than per year; the true-up mechanism described in operational detail; the term end checked against the season; no claim that a seasonal pattern will repeat; no annualised cost figure invented.
depth.summary: Seasonality is a timing problem that fixed obligations convert into a solvency problem in specific weeks. The transferable method is to place every obligation on the same calendar as the receipts, count the tight periods, and choose a structure whose mechanics are documented rather than described. The same reasoning applies to hiring a seasonal workforce, signing a lease with stepped rent, or committing to a fixed software contract: the question is never whether the year covers it, but whether the month does.

lessons.title: Concentration: when one customer, processor or account carries the file
lessons.explanation: Concentration is dependence. It is not a fault in itself; nearly every small business depends on somebody. The analytical job is to identify the specific dependency, quantify it, and decide whether the funding structure can survive it. There are five kinds to test. Customer concentration: the largest customer's share of revenue, and the shape of the relationship behind it, including whether the contract renews at the customer's option. Processor concentration: the share of receipts flowing through one payment processor, and what happens to collections during a hold, a reserve increase or a processing interruption. Account concentration: whether all receipts and all debits sit in one bank account, so a single freeze or fraud event stops both sides of the ledger. Supplier or licensing concentration: a single vendor, franchisor, licence or certification without which the business cannot operate. Geographic concentration: one city, one weather event, one landlord. Each dependency converts into a specific structural answer. Customer concentration may call for a smaller advance, a shorter term, a reserve, or collateral outside the concentration. Processor concentration may call for a second processor before funding and a stated rule about notice if the arrangement changes. Account concentration may call for a separate operating account for the obligations, or for the merchant to demonstrate the ability to move collections. Supervision thinks about concentration explicitly: the OCC's asset-based lending booklet treats receivables that exceed concentration limits as commonly ineligible for the borrowing base, alongside delinquency, affiliate receivables that may deteriorate together, and re-aged receivables whose collection probability has fallen. The lesson for a funder is the same one a bank applies: identify the exposure, decide what is not eligible, and document the decision rather than discovering it after a problem.
lessons.example: Meridian Fabrication has annual revenue of $980,000, of which $607,600, or 62 percent, comes from one manufacturer. Eligible accounts receivable total $220,000 on the latest aging. The largest customer's receivable is $136,400 and the other customers account for $83,600. Under a borrowing base that excludes receivables exceeding a 25 percent concentration limit, the limit for a single obligor is $55,000, so $81,400 of the largest customer's receivable is ineligible and eligible receivables fall to $138,600. At an 80 percent advance rate against eligible receivables, availability is $110,880. Ignoring the concentration limit produces $176,000, an overstatement of $65,120, or 58.7 percent more availability than the aging supports. The same file has a second dependency: 96 percent of receipts arrive through one processor. A six-day hold on settlements would delay approximately $16,371.43 at the observed weekly rate of $19,100, which is more than the merchant's entire weekly fixed cost. Neither fact makes Meridian unfundable. Together they set the terms of an honest recommendation: an advance sized against $110,880 rather than $176,000; a requirement that notices from the processor be shared within a stated period; a reserve equal to at least one week of receipts; and, if the largest customer's share keeps rising, a decision point written into the file rather than left to the next renewal.
lessons.question: A merchant explains that one customer is 62 percent of revenue but has been with them for eleven years, so the concentration is safe. How should that be treated?
lessons.answer: Tenure is evidence about the relationship's durability, and it is worth recording. It does not remove the dependency: the exposure to be tested is what happens to repayment if that customer reduces, delays or stops, and the answer is expressed as a sizing and structure decision.
lessons.distractor: The eleven-year relationship resolves the concentration question, so no adjustment is needed to size or structure the facility, provided payment history is clean.
lessons.correction: A long relationship changes the probability, not the consequence. The consequence is that a single decision by that customer can stop most of the inflow that repays the obligation, and probability estimates do not survive that kind of single-point dependency on their own. Record the tenure, then size the facility so the trough after that customer's departure is survivable, and name the trigger that would change the recommendation.

depth.definitions: Concentration is the share of a defined total attributable to one counterparty, channel, account, supplier or location. An eligible receivable is one the funder will advance against; a concentration limit is the maximum share of the base that one obligor may represent. Dilution is the portion of receivables that will not be collected in full because of returns, allowances, disputes or credits. Re-aged receivables are balances whose ageing has been reset, often by taking a partial payment or a promise, and the OCC booklet treats them as commonly ineligible because the probability of collection has fallen. Affiliate receivables are amounts owed by related parties, which can deteriorate at the same time as the borrower and increase fraud potential in periods of financial stress. A reserve, or holdback, is an amount withheld from an advance and released on defined conditions. Processor concentration is the share of receipts settled through a single provider, and a processor hold is a delay or restriction on releasing settled funds.
depth.mechanism: Concentration matters because it correlates the borrower's inflow with a single decision or event, and correlated risk cannot be diversified by adding more of the same exposure. A borrowing base responds to this by removing the excess above a limit from eligible collateral, which lowers availability mechanically even though the asset still exists and may be collected in full. That is not pessimism about the customer; it is a statement that the funder is unwilling to lend twice against one payer, since a dispute with that payer can both stop new receipts and freeze the collection of the receivable already advanced against. The same logic applies to a single processor and a single bank account, with one addition: a processor hold or an account freeze is an operational event that can occur without any change in the merchant's business, so the mitigation is diversification or notice, not analysis. Concentration limits should be written with defined numbers and reviewed on a stated schedule, because a limit that moves whenever a merchant asks is not a limit. The final step is a decision rule: at what measured share does the recommendation change, what would the change be, and who will notice that the threshold was crossed.
depth.secondExample: A dental practice and a metal finisher both have a 62 percent concentration, and the difference is what sits behind it. The practice's concentration is a patient population described in aggregate, spread across hundreds of individuals in one locality, so the dependency is geographic and the practical risk is a local event such as a road closure or an employer's relocation. The finisher's concentration is a single purchase-order relationship with one manufacturer, renegotiated annually, where a decision by one procurement team removes most of next year's revenue. Both files show the same percentage and require different answers: the practice's exposure can be mitigated by sizing against the local economy and shortening the term, while the finisher needs a reserve, a lower advance multiple and a documented trigger tied to the customer's order volume. The mechanism to carry forward is that percentages are comparable while the structures behind them are not, so a concentration analysis that stops at the number has done half the work.
depth.mistake: The most frequent error is treating concentration as a character question about the customer, so a well-known or longstanding name is used to dismiss the dependency; the correction is to convert the relationship into a scenario, for example a thirty percent reduction in that customer's orders, and to state what the repayment schedule looks like in that scenario. A second error is measuring concentration only on revenue while ignoring the receivable side, where a concentration limit can quietly cut availability by more than half. A third is ignoring a second, less obvious concentration such as a single processor, a single account or a licence held by one individual, so the file looks diversified on the customer axis and is fragile on another. A fourth is accepting a concentration limit figure without asking who set it, when it was set, and what the file would look like at a different figure, which makes the limit an assumption rather than a decision.
depth.application: Optional task: take a fictional aging, compute eligible receivables under a stated concentration limit, compare availability with and without the limit, and write the recommendation in three sentences. Model response: 'The largest customer is $136,400 of $220,000 in receivables and 62 percent of revenue. At a 25 percent limit the single-obligor cap is $55,000, leaving $138,600 eligible and $110,880 of availability at an 80 percent advance rate; without the limit the same aging suggests $176,000, which overstates availability by $65,120. I would size against the limited base, ask for a second processor and a written plan for sharing processor notices, and set a review point if that customer's share rises further.' Self-review: the limit and advance rate both stated as assumptions; the arithmetic shown; a named non-customer dependency identified; a documented trigger for changing the recommendation; no claim that the customer will stay or that the limit can be waived on request.
depth.summary: Concentration is the study of single points of failure and what they justify structurally. The transferable method is to name the dependency, quantify it in dollars and percentages, remove the unacceptably correlated portion from what you will lend against, and write a decision rule for the next review. The same method applies to a funder's own portfolio, where the OCC's concentration guidance exists precisely because a portfolio can behave like one large exposure, and to any operating decision where one supplier, one channel or one person carries too much of the outcome.

lessons.title: Needs analysis before product: amount, duration, source and timing
lessons.explanation: A product is an answer, and an answer without the question is a guess with a price attached. The needs analysis is the question, and it has five parts. Use of funds: what specifically will the money buy or pay, item by item, with amounts. Duration of need: how long that use will consume or tie up the money, because inventory that turns in four months and a machine with a seven-year life are different durations even when the dollar amounts match. Timing: when the money must be in hand, and whether a delay changes the cost of the underlying purchase. Amount: the sum of the uses plus fees and a stated contingency, and no more. Source of repayment: the specific inflow that will pay the obligation, expressed in the merchant's own cycle, with the concentration and seasonality work from the preceding lessons applied. Only after those five are written does product selection begin, and the selection has to be checked against program constraints rather than sales preference. The SBA's 7(a) program lists permissible uses including working capital, equipment, real estate, refinancing current business debt and changes of ownership, while the 504 program is narrower: SBA states that a 504 loan cannot be used for working capital or inventory and cannot be used to consolidate, repay or refinance debt that does not meet the definition of qualified debt. Those are not marketing distinctions; they are the boundary lines of the answer. Building the analysis first also produces the number that most conversations skip: the cost of the wrong structure. Inventory financed over a term longer than its turnover concentrates cost without adding capacity, and a piece of equipment financed on a schedule shorter than its working life converts a capital purchase into a cash-flow problem. The needs analysis is also the document that makes a smaller recommendation defensible, which is often the most valuable output of the exercise.
lessons.example: A bakery requests $120,000: $70,000 of flour, sugar, butter and packaging for a six-month wholesale contract, and $50,000.37 for a laminating line. The needs analysis separates them. The ingredient purchase is a working-capital need of roughly six months, repaid by the contract receipts. The laminator is a seven-year asset. Financed as a single advance at a factor of 1.32 over forty weeks, the $120,000 advance carries a total repayment amount of $158,400, a difference of $38,400, collected at $3,960 a week. Financed as two matched instruments, the working-capital portion might be a line drawn for six months at twelve percent, costing $4,200 for the period, and the equipment could be a sixty-month term at 8.5 percent with a payment of $1,025.83 and total interest of $11,549.80 over the sixty payments. The combined cost of the matched structure is $15,749.80, against $38,400 for the single advance, and each figure is a dollar amount with dates, not a rate comparison. Two further observations belong in the recommendation. First, the equipment portion at $50,000.37 is below the working-capital portion, so if the wholesale contract is delayed, the honest recommendation is to fund only the equipment and re-run the analysis when the contract is signed, which is a $50,000.37 recommendation instead of $120,000. Second, the ingredient purchase has a quantity risk: if the contract is cancelled, the inventory may not be resalable at cost, so the structure should include a shorter draw period or a reserve that reflects that specific exposure.
lessons.question: A merchant asks for $150,000 to buy inventory, renovate a leased space and pay a deposit on a delivery van, all on one schedule. What does a needs analysis require before any product is discussed?
lessons.answer: Separate the uses by duration and security: inventory turns quickly, the renovation improves leased premises that cannot secure the cost, and the van is a titled asset with a working life. Each has its own amount, duration, timing and repayment source, and the recommendation should be built per use rather than blended.
lessons.distractor: One blended advance is appropriate because the total amount is the same and a single schedule is simpler for the merchant to administer.
lessons.correction: Simplicity is a benefit that can be bought at the cost of fit. Blending means the shortest-lived use is financed on the longest schedule and the longest-lived asset on a schedule set by the shortest need, which raises total dollars paid without matching either. The correction is to write the uses separately with amounts and durations, then decide deliberately whether one instrument or several is honest.

depth.definitions: Use of funds is the itemised purpose, with an amount and a date for each item. Duration of need is the period over which the money is consumed, tied up or amortised. Source of repayment is the identified inflow that pays the obligation, in the merchant's own cycle and currency. Contingency is a stated allowance for cost variance, and it should be a number rather than an adjective. Term is the length of the obligation, and matched financing means the term corresponds to the life of the use. Advance is the amount provided; proceeds are what reaches the merchant after any deduction; the total repayment amount is the sum of all scheduled payments. A factor is a multiplier applied to the advance to produce the total repayment amount, and it is not an interest rate or an annual percentage rate. A guarantee is a separate obligation of another person or entity; collateral is property against which an interest is taken.
depth.mechanism: Two errors of fit drive most expensive structures. The first is duration mismatch, where short-lived uses are financed over long terms. The merchant pays the cost of the long term without gaining anything, and the obligation outlives the asset, so the schedule is still running when the inventory has been sold and the receipts spent. The second is amortisation mismatch on long-lived assets, where a machine with a ten-year life is repaid in eight months of debits, which converts a capital decision into a liquidity squeeze in the merchant's weakest quarters. Both are visible only when the analysis is written down. Programme rules then narrow the answer further, because some programmes cannot fund certain uses at all, so a recommendation that ignores those boundaries is not merely suboptimal; it is unavailable. Finally, the analysis forces the merchant to state the repayment source in words they recognise, which is the point at which many requests quietly change size. A recommendation that survives this process is more expensive to prepare and far cheaper to live with.
depth.secondExample: A plumbing company needs $85,000: a used box truck at $46,000, $24,000 of parts stocking for a maintenance contract, and $15,000 to cover the payroll gap created by switching from deposit-on-completion to net-thirty billing with a new commercial client. The truck is a titled asset with a stated useful life and is straightforward to match to a term. The parts stocking is a working-capital use of roughly four months, tied directly to the maintenance contract's schedule. The payroll gap is the interesting one, because it is a permanent change in working capital caused by payment terms, not a one-time hole: the correct analysis asks what the steady-state receivable balance must be to support thirty-day terms, and whether the company has it. If it does not, the honest recommendation may be to fund a smaller amount, hold the parts order until the contract's first payment, or renegotiate the terms to net fifteen with the client. Each of those answers is more useful than lending into a working-capital change whose size nobody has quantified.
depth.mistake: The standard mistake is working backwards from a product and constructing uses that fit it, which produces recommendations with a plausible surface and no internal arithmetic; the diagnostic is to remove the product from the conversation and ask what each dollar buys and when it is repaid. A second mistake is accepting the merchant's stated amount as the need, when the stated amount is frequently the amount of a previous offer or the amount the merchant believes will be approved; the correction is to build the itemised list and total it in front of the merchant. A third mistake is omitting the fees and the contingency, so the merchant completes the purchase with a shortfall and borrows again, which is how stacking begins. A fourth is treating a working-capital change caused by payment terms as a one-time hole, which understates the permanent funding requirement and produces a schedule the business cannot retire.
depth.application: Optional task: build a five-part needs analysis for a fictional merchant who asks for one blended amount, and write both the sized recommendation and the smaller alternative. Model response: 'Your $120,000 splits into $70,000 of ingredients with a six-month life and a $50,000.37 laminator with a seven-year life. On one schedule at a factor of 1.32 over forty weeks, the total repayment amount is $158,400, a difference of $38,400 at $3,960 a week. With the working-capital piece drawn at twelve percent for six months, about $4,200, and the laminator financed over sixty months at 8.5 percent, $1,025.83 a month and $11,549.80 of interest, the combined cost is $15,749.80 with the same assets. If the wholesale contract has not been signed, my recommendation is to fund the laminator only and re-run this when the contract is in hand.' Self-review: every use has an amount and a duration; the repayment source is named for each; both structures are described in dollars and dates; no annualised percentage is invented; the smaller recommendation is presented as a real option rather than a fallback; nothing implies an approval guarantee.
depth.summary: The needs analysis is the discipline that keeps a recommendation tied to a purpose. The transferable method is to itemise uses by amount and duration, state the source and timing of repayment, build the total including fees and contingency, and only then choose an instrument by fit. The same five questions govern equipment purchases, hiring plans and marketing spend, which is why the exercise pays for itself even when the answer is that no financing is needed.

questions.prompt: A file contains a clean UCC search result showing no financing statements naming the business, and a document from a prior funder whose financing statement names the owner personally. What has the search established?
questions.answer: It establishes that no perfected filing names the business entity, which is only part of the priority picture. The personal filing still needs to be read, checked for its status on the record, and accounted for in any guarantee or lien discussion.
questions.distractor: It establishes that the business has no liens at all, because a search naming the business returned nothing and the personal filing cannot attach to business assets.
questions.correction: Filing records are searched by debtor name, so a filing under an individual name will not appear in a search of the entity name. Read every name that could appear on a filing, check whether each is still effective under the five-year lapse and continuation rules, and document the result as a negative or positive finding with its date.

questions.prompt: Twelve weeks of statements show $284,600 of gross deposits, including $18,000 of owner transfers, $25,000 of equipment loan proceeds and $12,400 of transfers from a related account. Existing debits are $2,750 a week. What is the proposed $1,600 weekly remittance as a share of normalized deposits?
questions.answer: Normalized deposits are $229,200, or $19,100 a week, so $1,600 is 8.38 percent, and combined debt service of $4,350 is 22.77 percent.
questions.distractor: Normalized deposits are $284,600, or $23,716.67 a week, so $1,600 is 6.75 percent and combined debt service is 18.34 percent.
questions.correction: Gross deposits include credits that are not customer receipts. The three listed categories total $55,400 and must be removed before the ratio is computed. Using gross deposits understates the share of real operating receipts that the obligations consume, which is the kind of error that makes an unaffordable obligation look comfortable.

questions.prompt: Monthly receipts total $657,500, averaging $54,791.67, with a trough of $38,000 in February and a peak of $72,000 in July. A fixed $5,600 weekly schedule equals $24,266.67 a month. What does the season analysis show?
questions.answer: The obligation is 63.86 percent of February receipts and 33.70 percent of July receipts, and it exceeds 45 percent of receipts in six of twelve months, so the fixed schedule does not match the season.
questions.distractor: The obligation is 44.29 percent of average monthly receipts, which is within a normal range, so the schedule is acceptable as long as the annual total is covered.
questions.correction: The average is not a period. A fixed obligation is met from the receipts of the period in which it falls, so the test is per month and the count of tight months is the finding. Six difficult months is a structural mismatch; the responses available are a schedule sized to the trough, a scheduled pause, or a percentage structure with a documented true-up.

questions.prompt: Eligible receivables are $220,000, the largest customer owes $136,400 and represents 62 percent of revenue, and the borrowing base excludes receivables above a 25 percent single-obligor limit, advanced at 80 percent. What is availability with and without the limit?
questions.answer: With the limit the cap is $55,000, eligible receivables fall to $138,600 and availability is $110,880; without the limit it appears to be $176,000, an overstatement of $65,120.
questions.distractor: With the limit availability is $138,600 and without it $220,000, because the concentration limit applies to availability rather than to the eligible base.
questions.correction: The limit acts on the base before the advance rate is applied. Applying it after the advance rate confuses the two steps and changes the answer. Write the sequence explicitly, base then limit then advance rate, because that ordering is what makes the resulting number auditable.

questions.prompt: A bakery wants $120,000 for a six-month ingredient purchase and a seven-year laminator. What does the needs analysis require before a product is discussed?
questions.answer: Separate the two uses by amount, duration, timing and repayment source, since six months and seven years are different needs that should be matched to instruments rather than blended into one schedule.
questions.distractor: Present one blended $120,000 schedule, because the total amount is the same and a single payment stream is easier for the merchant to manage.
questions.correction: Blending means the short-lived use is financed on the longest available schedule and the machine on a schedule driven by the smaller need, which raises total dollars paid without adding capacity. The five-part analysis is written before instrument selection, and it is also what makes a smaller recommendation, such as funding only the laminator until the contract is signed, defensible.

units.title: Negotiating terms, distress conversations and accountable decisions

lessons.title: Covenants and personal guarantees in practice: what actually binds
lessons.explanation: A covenant is a promise inside a contract, and a guarantee is a separate promise by a person to answer for the debt of another. Both are placed in the middle of a sales conversation as if they were closing formalities, and both are the parts most likely to be misunderstood by the merchant later. The practical work is translation. Start with what the covenant actually does: a reporting covenant governs what must be sent and by when; an availability covenant sets a threshold below which the funder may take control of collections, which the OCC's asset-based lending guidance describes as springing dominion, a right the bank reserves and exercises when the borrower fails to meet a stated requirement such as an excess availability standard; a financial covenant sets a measured ratio or floor; a cross-default ties this obligation to another, so a default elsewhere accelerates this one. For each, the merchant's question is what happens on the day it is breached, how much notice exists, whether there is a cure period, and what the breach costs. Then translate the guarantee. An unlimited guarantee means the guarantor is answerable for the whole remaining obligation, not for a share, and when two people sign, the obligation is commonly joint and several, so the funder may pursue either one for the full amount. A guarantee is generally not released because the guarantor sells their interest in the business, and it is a separate instrument from the lien, so the two must be discussed separately: the lien is what the funder can take, and the guarantee is who owes if the taking falls short. Negotiation, when it is available at all, is about the specific terms that change outcomes: whether a guarantee is capped in dollars, whether it is limited to a percentage of the outstanding balance, whether the funder must exhaust collateral first, whether a personal residence is included, and whether cash collateral or a reserve can substitute for part of the exposure. None of those can be promised casually, and none should be described as non-negotiable when it has not been asked. The single line that must never be said is that a guarantee or an upfront fee will not be required, because the FTC's action against RAM Capital Funding concerned allegations that the defendants required personal guarantees and upfront fees after representing they would not, along with debiting more than stated.
lessons.example: A merchant signs a $60,000 advance with a total repayment amount of $66,000 collected at $2,750 a week over twenty-four weeks, guaranteed by two owners. At week twenty the merchant has paid $55,000 and the remaining obligation is $11,000. If the business stops paying, that $11,000 is the starting point for the guarantors, and because the guarantee is joint and several, either owner can be pursued for the full remaining balance and interest permitted by the documents, with the second owner's position between themselves and the first left to a separate arrangement between the two of them. The merchant's stated belief, that each owner answers for half, is wrong in law and in practice because the funder is not obliged to split its demand. The covenant side is equally concrete. Availability is modeled at $110,880 on the current borrowing base, and the agreement states that the funder may take control of collections when availability falls to fifteen percent of the commitment, which is $16,632. The merchant asks whether that threshold can be lowered to ten percent: the arithmetic is to show what availability of $11,088 would imply about eligible collateral, and to note that a lower threshold delays a control event rather than preventing one. A filing taken on 2026-03-01 remains effective for five years, until 2031-03-01, and a continuation can be filed only within the six months before expiration, beginning 2030-09-01, so a lapse is a lapse in the funder's protection and never a release of the merchant's obligation. All of these figures are fictional illustrations of structure and are not terms of any actual agreement.
lessons.question: An owner says they were told the personal guarantee would be capped at half the advance because there are two owners. What is the honest response?
lessons.answer: That the guarantee documents determine this, and that a joint and several unlimited guarantee lets the funder pursue either guarantor for the full remaining obligation. If a cap or a limited guarantee is wanted, it has to be requested and written into the documents before signing, and it may not be available.
lessons.distractor: That the split happens automatically once two owners sign, because the funder must act reasonably and cannot collect more from one guarantor than that owner's share of the business.
lessons.correction: Nothing in a joint and several guarantee allocates the funder's claim between guarantors; allocation is a matter between the guarantors, and the funder's documents govern who can be pursued for how much. Read the guarantee, ask what is limited and what is not, and never describe a guarantee's scope from memory.

depth.definitions: A covenant is a promise in the loan or advance agreement. A reporting covenant specifies documents and deadlines. A financial covenant is a measured test such as a minimum coverage or liquidity figure. An availability covenant sets a threshold on a borrowing base. Dominion is control over collections; full dominion applies proceeds continuously, and springing dominion reserves the right to apply them when the borrower fails a stated requirement. A guarantee is a promise to answer for another's obligation; a limited guarantee caps the amount or percentage; an unlimited guarantee does not; joint and several means each guarantor can be pursued for the whole. A security interest is an interest in property, perfected in most cases by filing a financing statement. Recourse is the right to look beyond the collateral to the obligor or guarantor.
depth.mechanism: The mechanism worth understanding is the interaction between control of collections and the guarantee, because together they decide what actually happens in a stress case. When a covenant is breached and the funder exercises dominion, all receipts are applied against the advance until the condition is cured, which immediately reduces the merchant's working cash even though nothing about their trading has changed. That is why an availability threshold is not a technicality and why a merchant should know the number, the notice period and the cure route in advance. The guarantee sits behind that process as the answer to any shortfall after collateral is realised. Because the guarantee is usually unconditional, it does not depend on the funder first exhausting the business's assets, unless the documents say so, and because it is often joint and several, the funder's collection strategy may target whichever guarantor has assets. Negotiating well means changing the instrument rather than the tone: a dollar cap, a percentage limitation, a requirement to exhaust collateral, an exclusion of a primary residence, or a substitute reserve. Each has a cost, and the merchant should hear what the funder is giving up in exchange.
depth.secondExample: Consider two merchants with identical $50,000 advances and identical guarantees, but different covenant packages. The first agreement carries only a reporting covenant and no financial or availability test, with a lower advance multiple and a reserve of two weeks of receipts. The second carries a coverage covenant tested quarterly, a springing dominion threshold at ten percent availability, and a cross-default to the merchant's equipment loan, with a higher advance multiple and no reserve. The second looks better on price and on amount, and it is measurably more fragile: one slow quarter trips a covenant and triggers control of collections, and a missed payment on the equipment loan accelerates the advance. Neither package is dishonest, and the choice between them is a real trade of price against constraint. The point of a covenant review is to make that trade visible before signature, so the merchant can decide whether the larger advance is worth the tighter trigger, rather than discovering the trade in the month the covenant is breached.
depth.mistake: The most damaging error is a reassurance about guarantees or fees that is not in the documents, which is precisely the conduct the RAM Capital Funding allegations describe. Sales language such as this is standard or nobody actually enforces that should never be used. A second error is reading covenants as boilerplate and never telling the merchant the number that triggers control of collections, which leaves them surprised at the worst moment. A third error is treating the lien and the guarantee as the same thing, which hides who remains liable when the collateral is worth less than the balance. A fourth is assuming a filing stays effective forever: five-year effectiveness and a continuation window limited to the six months before expiration mean a lapsed filing can leave a funder unperfected, and a merchant should never be told that a lapse cancels what they owe.
depth.application: Optional task: translate a fictional agreement into a one-page merchant briefing with four rows: reporting, financial, availability and cross-default, plus a separate guarantee row. Model response: 'Reporting: monthly statements by the fifteenth and processor reports weekly. Financial: coverage tested each quarter; if it falls below the stated figure we would discuss a cure plan. Availability: if availability falls to fifteen percent of the commitment, which on today's base is $16,632, the funder may take control of collections until the condition is cured. Cross-default: a missed payment on your equipment loan can affect this advance. Guarantee: unlimited and joint and several, so either guarantor can be pursued for the full remaining balance; a dollar cap would need to be requested and agreed in writing, and I will ask, but I cannot promise it.' Self-review: every commitment restated as a number, a date or a document; the guarantee and the lien described separately; no statement that a guarantee will not be required; no implication that a covenant will not be enforced.
depth.summary: Covenants and guarantees are where a relationship is actually governed. The transferable habit is to convert each clause into an event: what triggers it, who acts, what notice and cure exist, and what it costs. The same habit applies to leases, franchise agreements and supplier contracts, and it is the difference between a merchant who is surprised by an agreement and one who negotiated it.
