lessons.title: Renewal, refinance and consolidation: the honest test for each
lessons.explanation: Three words that describe three different transactions, and the funding industry uses them interchangeably in a way that hides who benefits. A renewal is a new advance to an existing client, often before the previous one has finished. A refinance is the replacement of one obligation with another whose structure is better matched to the use or the cash flow. A consolidation is the combining of several obligations into one. Each can be legitimate, and each has a version that is not. The test has four parts, and all four are about dollars and dates rather than adjectives. First, list the obligations before and after, with every payment date and every amount, including fees. Second, compute the total dollars that will leave the merchant's account under the old path and the new one, to the end of both schedules. Third, ask whether the merchant's position improves in cash terms, not merely in convenience: more dollars to the merchant, a longer matched term, a lower total amount paid, or a reduced peak obligation in the merchant's weak season. Fourth, identify the incentive of the person recommending it, because a renewal typically generates a new fee on the full funded amount, which means the recommendation to renew arrives with a payment attached to it. A renewal that funds a genuine need, disclosed with the cost of the old obligation still on the books, is legitimate. A renewal that exists to reset fees and extend the merchant's obligation, offered during a week when the merchant is short because the previous schedule was too large, is the classic pattern the FTC staff perspective describes as stacking, where a merchant encumbers the same receipts more than once in order to meet obligations and stay open. The honest version of a renewal names the total obligation now outstanding, the new total after the renewal, and the combined dollars the merchant will pay if nothing changes. Consolidation deserves the same arithmetic, with one addition: the merchant should be told which obligations are being paid off, in what amounts, and what evidence will confirm each payoff, because a consolidation that leaves one obligation in place while collecting for both is not a consolidation.
lessons.example: A merchant took a $40,000 advance with net proceeds of $38,400 after $1,600 of fees, a total repayment amount of $52,000 and twenty weekly payments of $2,600. At week fourteen the merchant has paid $36,400 and $15,600 remains, with six weeks to run. The merchant needs $30,000 more for a second location and the funder offers a renewal: a new $52,000 advance with $15,600 used to pay off the old one, leaving $36,400 of new proceeds, a total repayment amount of $68,640 at $2,860 a week over twenty-four weeks, and a new dollar cost of $16,640. Comparing paths from week fourteen: finishing the old obligation costs $15,600 and then, if the $30,000 is still needed, a fresh advance of $30,000 at a factor of 1.32 would carry a total of $39,600, so total dollars after week fourteen are $55,200. The renewal path takes $68,640 from the merchant's account for the same underlying need, $13,440 more, or 24.35 percent. The honest refinance alternative in the same week is a $30,000 term obligation at nine percent over thirty-six months, with a payment of $953.99 a month, total payments of $34,343.64 and $4,343.64 of interest, which is a smaller monthly burden and a much smaller total. Viewed over the whole relationship, the original $52,000 plus the renewal's $68,640 is $120,640, against $86,343.64 for the original plus the matched term. The numbers do not prove that a renewal is always wrong; they show what the merchant is buying, which is speed and proceeds today at the cost of a larger total and a longer obligation. All figures are fictional illustrations of arithmetic, and the comparison is stated in dollars and dates rather than as a rate.
lessons.question: A merchant is offered a renewal that pays off the existing advance and provides new money, described as a consolidation to make life easier. What must the recommendation actually show?
lessons.answer: The obligations before and after with their dates, the total dollars that leave the account under each path to the end of each schedule, the evidence that each old obligation is paid off, and the cost the merchant is accepting for the speed and proceeds today. If the merchant's position does not improve in dollars or in matched term, that has to be said.
lessons.distractor: A comparison of the two weekly payment amounts, because a renewal that lowers the weekly payment frees cash flow and therefore improves the merchant's position by definition.
lessons.correction: A smaller weekly payment over a longer schedule usually means a larger total, so it can improve this week's cash and worsen the position overall. The comparison has to run to the end of each schedule and show the total, with the old obligations itemised so the merchant can see what is being retired and what is not.

depth.definitions: A renewal is a new advance to an existing client, sometimes with the previous balance paid off inside it. A refinance replaces an obligation with one of different structure or term. A consolidation combines several obligations into one. The total repayment amount is the sum of all scheduled payments, including the amount advanced and the cost. Net proceeds are what reaches the merchant after fees, payoffs and any reserves. Stacking describes financing that encumbers the same receipts more than once, and it is a mechanism rather than an insult: it happens when a merchant needs money to meet an existing schedule. A payoff letter is a dated statement from a funder showing the amount required to retire an obligation, and it belongs in the file before any consolidation is described as complete.
depth.mechanism: The economics that make renewals attractive to a funder and expensive to a merchant are timing and base. A renewal computes fees on the full new advance rather than on the incremental money, and it restarts the schedule, so the merchant's obligation extends from the point where the old one was nearly finished. The merchant's decision is usually made under time pressure, in a week when the old schedule has taken most of the available cash, which is exactly when a new advance looks like relief. The analytic answer is not to refuse renewals; it is to separate two questions that the conversation tends to merge. The first is whether there is a genuine need, and how much money is needed for it. The second is whether this is the cheapest honest way to meet that need, given the merchant's cash pattern and the alternatives available. Answering both requires the totals, the dates and the payoffs, which is why a recommendation that contains no total repayment amount cannot be evaluated. Where an existing obligation is costly and the merchant has stable cash flow, a refinance into a matched term may reduce both the monthly burden and the total, and that option should be raised even when it pays the recommender less.
depth.secondExample: A different merchant has three separate obligations: a card advance being collected daily at a hundred and twenty dollars, an equipment loan at $610.42 a month, and a merchant advance being collected weekly at $1,450. Total obligations are high and the payment days collide. An honest consolidation here has a clear, checkable shape. It names each obligation with its current balance and its payoff figure, obtains payoff letters, repays all three, and replaces them with one obligation whose total dollars are lower than the sum of the remaining totals and whose payment dates avoid the merchant's weakest week. A dishonest version has the same form and different contents: it leaves the equipment loan in place and adds the new obligation on top, it does not obtain payoff letters, and it presents the new weekly payment as lower than the sum of the old ones without disclosing the total. The distinguishing evidence is documentary rather than rhetorical, which is why the file, the payoff letters and the total figures are the test rather than the word consolidation.
depth.mistake: The recurring error is comparing weekly payments between a short original schedule and a longer renewal schedule, which always favours the longer one and hides the total. The correction is to compute totals to the end of each schedule and to state the difference in dollars. A second error is describing a payoff without obtaining a payoff letter, which leaves the merchant exposed to a balance that survives the consolidation, including the possibility that a financing statement remains of record. A third is offering a renewal during a cash shortfall without disclosing that the shortfall may be caused by the original obligation being set too large, which turns a symptom into a new sale. A fourth is presenting a refinance as an improvement without checking that the new term matches the underlying use, since a longer term on short-lived working capital raises the total without adding capacity.
depth.application: Optional task: given a mid-life advance and a new need, compute the two paths in dollars and dates and write the recommendation. Model response: 'You owe $15,600 with six weeks to run. If you finish that schedule and then take $30,000 at a factor of 1.32, the total from here is $55,200. The renewal on offer would collect $68,640 from your account, which is $13,440 more, or 24.35 percent, in exchange for the money arriving this week rather than in six. A $30,000 term over thirty-six months at nine percent would be $953.99 a month and $34,343.64 in total payments. I can present the renewal, and I would rather you chose it knowing these three figures; my recommendation is the matched term if the second location can wait six weeks.' Self-review: totals computed to the end of each schedule; the payoff amount shown; the recommender's own compensation disclosed where relevant; no annualised rate invented; no guarantee of approval; the option that pays the recommender least is still presented.
depth.summary: Renewal, refinance and consolidation differ in what they replace and what they cost, and the test is always the same: obligations before and after with dates, totals to the end of each schedule, evidence of payoff, and the incentive behind the recommendation. The transferable habit is to convert any restructuring proposal into a before-and-after ledger, which applies equally to refinancing a mortgage, renegotiating a supplier contract, or rolling a balance onto a new card.

lessons.title: Collections, workouts and restructuring conversations under stress
lessons.explanation: When a merchant falls behind, the conversation becomes the product. What goes wrong is rarely a shortage of goodwill; it is a shortage of structure, a shortage of documentation, and occasionally conduct that crosses into illegality. The structure part has vocabulary worth learning precisely, because it decides who has discretion. An accommodation is any agreement to defer one or more payments, make a partial payment, forbear delinquent amounts, modify the contract, or provide other relief to a borrower in financial difficulty. A workout takes forms that include renewing or extending terms, extending additional credit, or restructuring with or without concessions. Supervision treats these as legitimate: the interagency policy statement states that institutions implementing prudent accommodation and workout arrangements after performing a comprehensive review of a borrower's financial condition will not be subject to criticism for doing so, even if the modified loans carry weaknesses. The practical consequence for a funder or an advisor is that a well-documented accommodation is an available answer, and that the comprehensive review is the price of using it. The documentation part is the discipline of putting the merchant's position on paper: arrears, the cause, the revised schedule, the new end date, what changes if a payment is missed again, and what the merchant must send to demonstrate performance. The conduct part is where boundary lines sit. Collateral must be handled in a commercially reasonable manner at every step, including method, timing and price, which is the standard UCC Article 9 sets for disposition after default. Threats, misstatements about what a funder can do, or communicating with third parties about a merchant's debt are the kinds of conduct that produce complaints and, in the cases regulators have brought, liability. Two scope points deserve care rather than confidence. First, the federal consumer debt-collection statute defines its terms around a consumer and a debt incurred primarily for personal, family or household purposes, so business debt sits largely outside it while a personal guarantee signed by a natural person may draw in state collection regimes and the reasoning of consumer-protection law more broadly. Second, none of this is legal advice, and any specific question about enforceability, filing priority or a merchant's rights belongs with a lawyer. What an advisor can do without hesitation is be accurate: state the balance, state the dates, state what the documents permit, state what happens next, and put it in writing.
lessons.example: A merchant is three weekly payments of $2,450 behind, a cure requirement of $7,350, plus a $250 fee recorded in the agreement, so the amount needed to bring the account current is $7,600. The remaining balance after the cure is $22,300, which at the current rate of $2,450 a week had 9.10 weeks to run. The merchant cannot pay the full cure and asks for relief. The accommodation that satisfies the review requirement starts with the review: sixty days of statements, a current ageing, an explanation of the cause, and a projection of the specific inflow that will restore the payments. On that basis a forbearance of eight weeks at $1,150 a week is documented. Eight weeks at $1,150 collects $9,200, leaving $13,100. At the restored rate of $2,450 a week that is 5.35 weeks, so the schedule needs six more weeks, with a final payment smaller than the others, and the total extension is fourteen weeks from today against the 9.10 weeks that remained. Nothing about the obligation's total changes; the time does, and the merchant's cash in the next two months rises by $1,300 a week. If instead the merchant stops paying entirely, the discussion turns to collateral. An illustration makes the stakes concrete: appraised orderly liquidation value of $31,000 against a forced sale outcome of $18,000 is a $13,000 difference, which is why the commercially reasonable standard in UCC 9-610 exists and why every step, including the method, the marketing and the timing, should be documented as it happens. Throughout, the advisor's script stays the same: here is your balance, here is what the documents say, here is the relief available if these conditions are met, and here is who can help you with the legal question, which is not me.
lessons.question: A merchant in distress asks whether they can stop paying and let the funder take the assets instead, and whether hiding a new account would help. What is the correct response?
lessons.answer: Explain the consequences accurately, including that collateral disposition is conducted under a commercially reasonable standard and any shortfall can still be claimed against the guarantors, and refuse to assist with concealment or with any statement that would mislead. Offer to route the legal question to a lawyer, and put the accommodation options in writing.
lessons.distractor: Explain that surrendering the assets ends the matter, because a funder that takes the collateral cannot pursue anyone further once it has realised the value.
lessons.correction: Surrender rarely ends the file. Disposition proceeds are applied against the balance, and a shortfall commonly remains enforceable against guarantors. Concealment is worse than unhelpful: it can convert a commercial problem into allegations of fraud and can defeat the relief the merchant is asking for. The only defensible path is accurate information, written options, and a referral for legal advice.

depth.definitions: Arrears are amounts past due. A cure is the action that restores the account to current, defined by the documents. Forbearance is an agreed suspension or reduction of payments without changing the total obligation. A modification changes terms such as the rate, the schedule or the maturity. A workout is the broader process of restructuring a relationship in difficulty. A shortfall is the difference between what the obligation requires and what realisation of collateral produces. Commercially reasonable is the statutory standard for disposing of collateral, covering the method, manner, time, place and other terms. A guarantor is a person or entity separately liable. The federal consumer collection statute's terms are defined around a consumer and a debt incurred primarily for personal, family or household purposes, so the statute's coverage does not extend to ordinary commercial obligations in the way many people assume, while other regimes and state law may apply.
depth.mechanism: Two mechanisms decide whether a workout succeeds. The first is that relief has to be temporary and conditional to be credible. An accommodation that simply lowers payments without a defined end, a restored schedule and a condition for performance is a deferral of the same crisis, and the funder's discretion to withdraw it tends to be exercised at the worst moment for the merchant. Writing the end date, the restored amount and the evidence of performance into the agreement converts goodwill into a term. The second is that the review is what makes the relief defensible, in both directions: the funder gets a documented basis for the decision, and the merchant gets a schedule that reflects actual capacity rather than hope. On the collateral side, the mechanism is price discovery. A disposition conducted quickly, without marketing and without a documented rationale, typically returns less, and the difference lands on the guarantor. Because the standard is applied to every aspect of the disposition, contemporaneous records of what was done and why are the funder's protection and the merchant's remedy.
depth.secondExample: A restaurant and a trucking company both fall behind by four weeks, and the same relief package produces different outcomes. The restaurant's problem is a slow season with a known end, so a two-month interest-only or reduced-payment accommodation with a restored schedule in the ninth week fits the cause: receipts return and the schedule resumes. The trucking company's problem is the loss of a contract that supplied 41 percent of its revenue and will not return, so reducing payments merely postpones an outcome the arithmetic already settled. The honest conversation there is about a smaller obligation, an asset sale, an orderly wind-down over a defined period, or a referral to a specialist adviser, rather than a forbearance that both parties know cannot be repaid. The distinguishing work is the same in both cases and it comes before the offer: identify whether the cause of the shortfall is temporary, structural or terminal, because the answer selects the instrument.
depth.mistake: The commonest mistake is offering relief before performing the review, which produces a schedule the merchant cannot meet and a second default that damages credibility on both sides. The correction is to require the documents first, even when that delays relief by a few days. A second mistake is describing a funder's powers inaccurately, either to pressure the merchant or to comfort them; both are misstatements about a legal instrument and both create exposure. A third is treating a business obligation as if consumer collection rules applied, or as if they certainly did not, without checking the jurisdiction and the personal guarantee involved. A fourth is letting collateral be disposed of without a documented commercial rationale, which converts a recoverable shortfall into a dispute about the shortfall's size.
depth.application: Optional task: draft a one-page accommodation memo for a fictional arrears case, suitable for being sent to the merchant and kept in the file. Model response: 'Your account is $7,600 behind, being three weekly payments of $2,450 plus a $250 fee recorded in the agreement, and $22,300 remains after that cure. Based on the sixty days of statements and the ageing you provided, we can document eight weeks at $1,150 a week, which collects $9,200 and leaves $13,100, then six weeks at the restored $2,450 with a smaller final payment, extending the schedule from 9.10 weeks to fourteen. If a payment is missed during the forbearance, we will review before deciding, and we will tell you in writing what the options are. Questions about your legal rights should go to a lawyer, and I can give you the names of free small-business advisers in your area.' Self-review: no threats, no statements about powers beyond the documents; the cause of the shortfall identified as temporary or structural; every number dated; the legal question referred out; nothing that could be read as advice to conceal or misstate.
depth.summary: Distress conversations are governed by structure, documentation and accuracy. The transferable method is to identify whether the cause is temporary, structural or terminal, build relief that is temporary and conditional, document it, and handle collateral and communications by the standard the law sets rather than by what feels expedient. The same discipline applies to a customer who cannot pay an invoice, a supplier in difficulty, or a landlord discussion, where the honest conversation about duration is usually the one that resolves the matter.

readings.note: Read 9-610(b), which requires every aspect of a disposition, including method, manner, time, place and other terms, to be commercially reasonable, and 9-610(c) on when a secured party may purchase collateral. Then read 9-609 for the right to take possession after default. This is the uniform text; the enacted version of the state whose law governs the agreement is what applies.

readings.title: 15 U.S. Code section 1692a - definitions of consumer, debt and debt collector
readings.note: Read the definitions of consumer, debt and debt collector. The definition of debt turns on a transaction entered into primarily for personal, family or household purposes, which is why ordinary commercial obligations are generally outside this federal consumer collection statute, while a personal guarantee by a natural person and state law can change the analysis. Read the definitions rather than assuming the coverage.

readings.title: New York Attorney General - Settlement with Yellowstone Capital regarding MCAs
readings.note: Read the section describing problems with other MCA companies and the guidance to merchants about filing complaints and consulting a lawyer, including the statement that the Attorney General cannot provide legal advice. Useful as a pointer to the complaint route a distressed merchant can use, and as an example of how collection conduct becomes a regulatory matter. The litigation against the remaining defendants is unresolved.

visual.title: Diagnose the cause, then choose the relief
visual.description: A decision flow that begins with the cause of the shortfall and routes to a specific relief structure, with a lower band showing what must be documented at each step and a side rail listing the conduct rules that apply throughout.
steps: Start box: compute arrears, the cure amount and the remaining balance, each with dates.
First branch: is the cause temporary, structural or terminal? Temporary routes to a dated short-term accommodation with a restored schedule.
Structural routes to a smaller obligation or a longer matched term with revised conditions; terminal routes to an orderly plan, asset realisation or an adviser referral.
Documentation band beneath the chosen path: statements, ageing, cause, revised schedule, restored amount, end date, and the consequence of a missed payment.
Collateral rail: for any realisation, record method, marketing, timing, price basis and decision-maker, because the standard applies to every aspect of the disposition.
Conduct rail: accurate balances, no threats, no third-party disclosure of the debt, written options, and a referral for legal questions.

lessons.title: Commission conflicts, disclosure and documenting a recommendation
lessons.explanation: A conflict of interest is not a moral failing; it is a structural fact about how someone is paid. When compensation rises with the size and cost of the product placed, the recommendation is made by a person whose income depends on the answer, and that arrangement produces predictable pressure whether or not the person feels it. The professional response has three parts: know the structure, disclose it, and document the reasoning that produced the recommendation. Knowing the structure means being able to state, for each option available, what the recommender is paid, when it is paid, and whether it is paid by the merchant, by the funder, or both. Some regimes address this directly. The SBA's conduct regulations define agents, packagers and referral agents, prohibit receiving compensation from both the applicant and the lender on the same loan except in a limited disclosure-based case, and treat an undisclosed business relationship between parties as good cause for losing the privilege to do business with the agency. They also make it a matter of good cause to give a guaranty that an application will be approved, or to imply that the work will involve special influence, and they require that a fee bear a necessary and reasonable relationship to the services actually rendered. Disclosure means telling the merchant, in plain words and before they commit, that the recommender is paid by the funder, the amount or the method, whether the same transaction could be placed elsewhere, and what the recommender would earn on the alternative they are recommending against. Disclosure is a sentence, not a gesture; it is stronger when it is written and kept. Documentation is the third part and the one that makes the other two auditable: a recommendation note that contains the needs analysis, the options considered with their dollar costs and dates, the option recommended and why, the conflicts disclosed, the risks, the conditions that would change the recommendation, and the date. The FTC's truth-in-advertising guidance supplies the standard for the words in that note, because a statement or an omission that is likely to mislead a reasonable person about something material is deceptive, materiality includes performance, price and the limits of what is promised, and a claim must have a reasonable basis before it is made. Applied to financing, this means no unsupported comparisons, no implied speed or approval that cannot be delivered, and no omission of a fee that a reasonable merchant would consider important.
lessons.example: A merchant needs $80,000 and a broker can place it with a funder paying three percent of the funded amount, which is $2,400, on a transaction at a factor of 1.35 over twenty-six weeks with a total repayment amount of $108,000 collected at $4,153.85 a week and a dollar cost of $28,000, equivalent to $35 per $100 of net proceeds. The same broker has a second option: $45,000 with a different funder paying one and a half percent, which is $675, on a transaction at a factor of 1.20 over twenty weeks with a total of $54,000 collected at $2,700 a week and a dollar cost of $9,000, equivalent to $20 per $100 of net proceeds. The compensation difference is $1,725, or 3.56 times, and the cost difference to the merchant, if the smaller amount meets the need, is $19,000. The disclosure script is short and specific: I am paid by the funder, three percent of the funded amount on the larger option and one and a half percent on the smaller one, so my firm earns $1,725 more if you take the larger one; here is why the needs analysis points to $45,000 for the equipment and the parts order, and here is what would change my view, which is a signed contract covering the additional volume. The recommendation note records the same figures, the two options, the reasoning, the disclosure and the conditions. If the merchant decides they want the larger amount for reasons of their own, the note records that the recommendation was the smaller option and that the merchant chose otherwise, which is a different document from a note that claims the larger amount was recommended.
lessons.question: A broker recommends the product that pays the highest commission and describes this as focusing on the client's best interest. What is wrong, and what must happen instead?
lessons.answer: The compensation structure creates a conflict that must be disclosed in specific terms, and the recommendation must be supported by a needs analysis and a comparison of costs in dollars and dates. Preferring the best-paying product may be defensible, but only if the reasoning, the alternatives and the compensation difference are disclosed and documented.
lessons.distractor: Nothing is wrong, because a higher-priced product usually offers a larger amount and longer term, which serves the client by giving them more capital and more flexibility.
lessons.correction: A larger amount and a longer term are not automatically better; they are different, and sometimes larger and longer cost more without meeting a need. The correction is procedural: state what is being paid, compare the options in dollars and dates, and write the reasoning. A recommendation that cannot survive that comparison should be replaced, whatever it pays.

depth.definitions: A conflict of interest exists when a personal or firm interest could influence a recommendation. Compensation disclosure is a statement of who pays the recommender and how much or by what method. Dual compensation means being paid by both the applicant and the lender for work on the same transaction; the SBA's conduct rules treat this as good cause for sanctions except in a narrow disclosed case. A fiduciary duty is a legal obligation to act in another's interest, and it is generally not imposed on commercial financing brokers by the federal rules discussed here, which is exactly why disclosure and documentation carry the weight. Documentation is the contemporaneous written record of the analysis, the options, the recommendation and the disclosure. Material, in the FTC's guidance, means information important to a person's decision. A reasonable basis means objective evidence that supports a claim before it is made.
depth.mechanism: Incentives work through selection and framing rather than through deliberate dishonesty. A recommender with a commission on funded amount will tend to present the options that can be funded, emphasise speed and proceeds, and be slow to raise the smaller structure that pays less, without any conscious decision to mislead. The remedy is procedural because intentions are not observable and processes are. Three practices change outcomes: recording every option with its dollar cost per hundred dollars of net proceeds, so the comparison is arithmetic rather than impression; disclosing the compensation on each option at the point the options are presented; and writing the recommendation with the conditions that would change it. Supervision reinforces the point from the other direction: the OCC's asset-based lending rating factors treat compensation structures skewed to loan and revenue production, with little evidence of incentives or accountability for loan quality, as a weakness. The same standard applies to an individual producer, where the test is whether the file shows a built-in check on production pressure.
depth.secondExample: Consider the same $80,000 request through two different channels. Through a broker paid three percent by the funder, the merchant receives one offer, presented as the best available, at a total repayment amount of $108,000 and $4,153.85 a week. Through a direct lender that pays its salesperson a salary and a small production bonus capped at a modest amount, the merchant receives two offers: a $45,000 facility matched to the equipment and inventory purchase, and an $80,000 facility at a total of $101,600 with $3,907.69 a week, with an explanation that the larger amount costs $22,400 more and is only needed if the second contract is signed. The arithmetic difference between the two $80,000 offers is $6,400, and the structural difference is that one channel disclosed the alternative and the other did not. A merchant who understands this can ask a single question of any recommender, which is what you are paid on each option and what you would earn on the smaller one, and can treat the answer as information about the process rather than as a judgement about the person.
depth.mistake: The commonest failure is a verbal assurance of impartiality with no numbers behind it, which does not disclose anything. The correction is to state the payer, the amount or method, and the difference between options. A second failure is omitting a fee or a condition from a comparison, which is an omission about something material and is exactly what the FTC's deception standard addresses. A third is recommending an amount that meets the recommender's funding minimum rather than the merchant's need, which is invisible unless the needs analysis is written down. A fourth is undocumented advice: when the only record is a call, a later dispute cannot be resolved by reference to what was said, and the merchant has no way to check whether the alternatives were considered.
depth.application: Optional task: write a two-paragraph recommendation note for a fictional merchant that discloses compensation and records a recommendation that pays the recommender less. Model response: paragraph one states the need and the analysis: $45,000 covers the equipment and parts order, with a total repayment amount of $54,000 at $2,700 a week for twenty weeks, a dollar cost of $9,000, which is $20 per $100 of net proceeds; the $80,000 option costs $28,000, which is $35 per $100, and is only needed if the additional contract is signed. Paragraph two discloses compensation: my firm is paid by the funder, one and a half percent of the funded amount on the $45,000 option and three percent on the $80,000 option, so we earn $1,725 more if you take the larger one; I am recommending the smaller amount, and I will revise this note if the contract arrives. Self-review: both options in dollars and dates; compensation stated per option; the conditions that would change the recommendation listed; no annualised rate invented; no approval or speed promised; the file retains the note with its date.
depth.summary: Conflicts are structural, so the response is procedural: know what you are paid, disclose it in specifics before commitment, and document an analysis that a reader could check. The transferable habit is to ask of any recommendation, including your own, who benefits from this option and what the alternative would cost me, then write down the answer. That habit travels to insurance, software procurement, real estate and any setting where commission and advice sit in the same conversation.

readings.title: 13 CFR Part 103 - Standards for Conducting Business with SBA: definitions, good cause for sanctions, dual compensation and fees
readings.note: Read the definitions in 103.1, then 103.4, including paragraph (b) on soliciting services where an undisclosed business relationship exists, paragraph (d) on implying special influence or giving a guaranty that an application will be approved, paragraph (e) on fees bearing a necessary and reasonable relationship to services rendered, and paragraph (g) on acting for both sides and receiving compensation from both without disclosure. Then read 103.5 on compensation agreements. These rules govern agents dealing with the SBA, and they are a concrete model of what disclosure means in a finance-intermediary setting.

readings.title: FTC - Advertising FAQ's: A Guide for Small Business (truth-in-advertising rules, deception and materiality, reasonable basis)
readings.note: Read the sections beginning 'What truth-in-advertising rules apply to advertisers?' and 'What makes an advertisement deceptive?'. The page states that an ad is deceptive if it contains a statement or omits information likely to mislead people acting reasonably and the information is material, that material claims include performance, features and price, and that advertisers must have a reasonable basis for claims before the ad runs. Written for advertising, and directly applicable to how a financing offer is described.

readings.title: OCC Comptroller's Handbook - Asset-Based Lending: rating factors on compensation and production incentives
readings.note: In Appendix D, read the rating factor that describes loan management and personnel compensation structures as providing an appropriate balance between loan and revenue production, loan quality and portfolio administration in a strong institution, and as skewed to production with little accountability for loan quality in a weak one. A supervisor's view of the same conflict this lesson asks you to disclose. Format note: a PDF served from the OCC site; the link was re-verified and is reachable. Read Appendix D's rating factors.

readings.title: FTC - 'Strictly Business' Forum Staff Perspective (February 2020): brokers, lead generators and unsupported claims
readings.note: Read the passage cautioning independent sales organisations, brokers and lead generators to avoid potentially false or unsubstantiated advertising claims, and the statement that a provider's use of marketing intermediaries does not immunise it from liability. It is staff perspective from February 2020, useful for the proposition that commission-driven channels carry responsibility for what they say.

visual.title: Option comparison with compensation disclosed
visual.description: A side-by-side comparison of every option available for one need, with the cost of each expressed in dollars and dates rather than rates, and a compensation row beneath each column that shows what the recommender earns on that option.
steps: Column per option, headed by the funded amount and the use it covers.
Row one: total repayment amount, with the payment amount and frequency beneath it.
Row two: dollar cost, and the same cost expressed per hundred dollars of net proceeds, so options are comparable without inventing a rate.
Row three: term and the number of payments, with the end date against the merchant's season.
Compensation row: who pays the recommender, the method, and the amount on that option, with the difference between options stated explicitly.
Footer: the recommended option, the reasoning, the conditions that would change it, and the date the note was written, signed by the recommender.

lessons.title: Capstone: a defensible recommendation, a clear decline and the conditions that would change it
lessons.explanation: A capstone case is not a harder arithmetic problem; it is the same skills applied in order, with a decision at the end and a written record of why. The order matters. Read the file as a claim ledger and mark the gaps. Normalise the deposits so the analysis runs on operating receipts rather than everything that reached the account. Put the receipts on a calendar and find the trough, then decide whether a fixed schedule fits it. Test concentration on customers, processors, accounts and licences. Write the needs analysis with amounts, durations, timing and sources of repayment. Match instruments to those needs and price each option in dollars and dates. Disclose compensation on each option. Then decide, and make the decision one that a colleague could review six months later without speaking to you. There are three possible decisions and all three are professional. Fund it as requested. Fund a smaller amount or a different structure with stated conditions. Decline, with reasons and with the conditions under which the answer would change. The third is the one that inexperienced advisors avoid, and it is usually the most valuable to the merchant, because a decline explained in terms of the analysis gives the merchant something to work on, while an approval that fails in four months gives them arrears and a damaged record. Two standards make a decline defensible. The first is specificity: Regulation B requires that a statement of reasons for adverse action be specific and indicate the principal reason or reasons, and it states that saying the decision was based on internal standards or policies, or that the applicant failed to achieve a qualifying score, is insufficient. That rule applies to creditors within its scope, and a funding professional working outside it should treat the specificity principle as the standard anyway, because it is the difference between an explanation and a brush-off. The second is honesty about causation: if the amount requested was too large for the trough, say so with the number; if concentration was the issue, say so with the percentage; if the gap was documentation, say what document closes it and when the answer would be reviewed. A decline that ends with a referral to free small-business advisors or a certified development company costs nothing and leaves the relationship intact.
lessons.example: A wholesale baker applies for a $2,450 weekly remittance against receipts that, after normalisation, run at $21,400 a week. The file is otherwise adequate: twelve months of statements, tax returns, documented ownership, a clean UCC search, one existing obligation at $2,100 a week, and a fixed cost base of $2,900 a week. Gross margin is 38 percent of receipts, so weekly contribution is $8,132. Total debt service under the request is $4,550, which is 21.26 percent of normalised receipts and 55.95 percent of contribution, and with fixed costs the coverage figure is $8,132 divided by $7,450, which is 1.09. That is a thin position before tax, before the winter trough, and before any of the concentration and seasonality findings, which show a trough-to-peak ratio of 0.53 and one customer at 62 percent of revenue. The defensible decision is a conditional counter-offer rather than a decline: a remittance of $1,900 a week, which with the existing obligation gives total debt service of $4,000, or 18.69 percent of receipts and 49.19 percent of contribution, and coverage of 1.18. If the merchant insists on $2,450 a week, the arithmetic says coverage falls to 1.09 and the answer is a decline with reasons, plus the conditions that would change it: eight weeks of statements showing contribution of at least $9,000 a week, the largest customer's share below 40 percent, no returned items in sixty days, and a second processor in place. As a check on the arithmetic, the largest remittance that reaches 1.15 coverage at the current contribution and fixed cost is $2,071.30. Every figure is a fictional illustration and none of it is an offer; the point is that the recommendation, the counter-offer and the decline conditions all come out of the same page of arithmetic.
lessons.question: A merchant fails the coverage test as requested but has a strong file otherwise. What is the most useful answer to give them?
lessons.answer: A specific arithmetic explanation with a conditional counter-offer, the number that would make the request work, and the conditions under which the answer would change, including what evidence is needed and when it would be reviewed.
lessons.distractor: A general statement that the file does not meet current criteria, with an invitation to apply again in three months when conditions improve.
lessons.correction: A general refusal gives the merchant nothing to act on and is the kind of non-explanation the Regulation B specificity standard rejects for covered creditors: internal standards are not a reason. The useful answer names the shortfall, shows the arithmetic, offers the size that works today, and lists the measurable conditions for revisiting it.

depth.definitions: A recommendation is a written statement of what should be done and why, with the conditions that would change it. A conditional counter-offer is a smaller or differently structured commitment tied to stated conditions. A decline is a decision not to fund, which should be accompanied by specific principal reasons and by the conditions under which it would be revisited. Coverage in this lesson is gross margin divided by combined obligations plus fixed operating cost, used as an illustrative test rather than a rule. Adverse action is an adverse decision on an application, and Regulation B sets notification content and timing for creditors within its scope, including the requirement that reasons be specific. Concentration is the share of a total attributable to one counterparty or channel. A trough-to-peak ratio compares the weakest and strongest periods of the year.
depth.mechanism: The reason a written record matters is that the decision is made under uncertainty and reviewed later with hindsight. A note that records the normalised receipts, the arithmetic, the conditions and the date allows an honest reconstruction: this was known, this was assumed, this was the trigger. Without it, the same decision is judged by its outcome, and an outcome that goes badly is read as a mistake regardless of the reasoning. The second mechanism is that decline conditions convert a no into a path. The merchant learns which single measurement controls the answer, and the funder or advisor gets a defined review point instead of a repeated conversation. The third is that a specific reason protects the merchant's ability to improve: an applicant told only that they did not meet criteria cannot tell whether the problem was size, season, concentration or documentation, and will often respond by applying elsewhere with the same file to a funder with lower standards, which is exactly the outcome an honest advisor should avoid.
depth.secondExample: A different merchant in the same trade has $21,400 of normalised weekly receipts and the same fixed costs, but a 44 percent gross margin and two customers at 24 percent each. Contribution is $9,416 a week, so the requested $2,450 remittance plus the existing $2,100 gives $4,550 against $7,450 of total obligations and fixed cost, a coverage figure of 1.26. The same request that was declined for the first merchant is fundable here, and the difference is entirely in the two inputs the analysis measured: margin and concentration. Nothing about the merchant's presentation or their urgency changed the answer, and nothing about the funder's appetite needed to be guessed at. This is the practical payoff of the whole level: the same arithmetic produces a decline, a counter-offer or a recommendation depending on measured facts, and the professional's job is to measure, write, and then say which one it is.
depth.mistake: The most common failure at the decision stage is deciding from the headline ask rather than the analysis, so the recommendation reflects the requested amount and a conversational impression rather than the trough, the contribution and the concentration findings. The correction is to re-read the arithmetic page before writing the recommendation. A second failure is a decline delivered without reasons or with reasons that are really restatements of policy, which is unhelpful and, for covered creditors, contrary to the specificity requirement. A third is a recommendation with no decline conditions, which leaves the merchant with no route back and the advisor with no review point. A fourth is documenting the recommendation after the merchant's decision rather than before, which produces a record shaped by the outcome and worthless as a check.
depth.application: Optional task: produce a one-page capstone record for a fictional merchant containing the file status, normalised receipts, season finding, concentration finding, needs analysis, options with costs, compensation disclosure, the recommendation with its arithmetic, and the decline or counter-offer conditions. Model response: 'Normalised receipts are $21,400 a week, contribution is $8,132 at a 38 percent gross margin, and existing obligations plus fixed cost are $4,550. The requested $2,450 remittance gives coverage of 1.09 against $7,450, with a trough-to-peak ratio of 0.53 and one customer at 62 percent of revenue. My recommendation is a counter-offer of $1,900 a week, which gives 1.18 coverage and total debt service at 18.69 percent of receipts; the largest remittance reaching 1.15 coverage is $2,071.30. If you need the larger amount, the answer today is no, and the file would be reviewed on delivery of eight weeks of statements showing contribution of at least $9,000 a week, a largest-customer share below 40 percent, no returned items in sixty days, and a second processor. I am paid by the funder at the rate stated on the comparison sheet, and the smaller option pays my firm less.' Self-review: every figure traceable; both a recommendation and decline conditions present; compensation disclosed; no approval or outcome promised; the reasons specific enough for a colleague to understand without a conversation.
depth.summary: A defensible decision is one whose reasoning is written down, whose arithmetic is visible, and whose conditions are stated so that the answer can change on evidence rather than on persistence. The transferable method is the sequence: verify, normalise, place on a calendar, test concentration, analyse the need, price the options, disclose compensation, decide, and write the conditions. That sequence is the whole of professional judgement in this field, and it applies to any decision made with incomplete information on someone else's behalf.

readings.title: CFPB - Regulation B, 12 CFR 1002.9 Notifications: business credit notifications and the specificity requirement
readings.note: Read paragraph (a)(3) on notification to business credit applicants, including the gross revenue threshold, and paragraph (b)(2), which requires that a statement of reasons be specific and indicate the principal reason or reasons, and states that citing internal standards or policies or a failure to achieve a qualifying score is insufficient. readings.title: SBA - Terms, conditions, and eligibility: eligibility requirements

Both are the kind of decisions a file must support with evidence, and both map onto the conditional counter-offer in this lesson.

readings.title: New York Attorney General - Settlement with Yellowstone Capital regarding MCAs
readings.note: Read the description of the claims and the relief, and the note that the litigation continues against other defendants. A reminder of why products must be described as they are and collections conducted accurately, and a pointer to the complaint route available to merchants. visual.title: The capstone decision page
visual.description: A single-page layout with the analysis on the left, the options and their costs in the middle, and the decision on the right. The decision box admits three outcomes, each with the arithmetic that supports it and the conditions attached.
steps: Left column, evidence block: file status, normalised weekly receipts, trough and peak with their ratio, and each concentration with its percentage.
Left column, analysis block: needs with amounts and durations, contribution, existing obligations and fixed cost.
Middle column: each option with its funded amount, total repayment amount, dollar cost per hundred dollars of net proceeds, term and end date, and compensation earned on that option.
Right column, decision box: fund as requested, counter-offer with conditions, or decline with specific principal reasons.
Beneath the decision: the arithmetic line that drives it, for example the remittance that reaches the stated coverage figure.
Footer: the measurable conditions that would change the answer, the date of the review, and the signature of the recommender.

questions.prompt: Two owners each hold 40 percent of a business and both sign an unlimited, joint and several guarantee on a $60,000 advance. At week twenty the remaining balance is $11,000 and the business stops paying. What is each owner's exposure?
questions.answer: Either owner can be pursued for the full remaining balance under a joint and several guarantee. How they divide it between themselves is a separate matter that the funder is not obliged to referee.
questions.distractor: Each owner is exposed to $5,500 because two guarantors split the obligation equally, which is what joint and several means in practice.
questions.correction: Joint and several means the funder may pursue any guarantor for the whole amount. The belief that signing with another person halves the exposure is one of the most consequential misunderstandings in small-business finance, and it is answered by reading the guarantee rather than by reasoning about fairness.

questions.prompt: At week fourteen a merchant has paid $36,400 of a $52,000 total repayment amount with payments of $2,600 a week, so $15,600 remains. A renewal advances $52,000, pays off the $15,600, leaves $36,400 and carries a total of $68,640. Finishing the old obligation and taking a fresh $30,000 at a factor of 1.32 totals $55,200. What does the comparison show?
questions.answer: The renewal takes $13,440 more, or 24.35 percent, from the merchant's account for the same need, in exchange for the money arriving immediately rather than in six weeks.
questions.distractor: The renewal is cheaper because the weekly payment falls from $2,600 to $2,860 spread over more weeks, which lowers the burden on the merchant's cash flow.
questions.correction: A weekly payment is not a total. $2,860 over twenty-four weeks is $68,640 collected, against $55,200 on the other path for the same need. Compute totals to the end of each schedule before comparing, and state the difference in dollars rather than in payment size.

questions.prompt: A merchant is three weekly payments of $2,450 behind, with a $250 recorded fee, and $22,300 remains after the cure. A forbearance of eight weeks at $1,150 is agreed. What is the rest of the schedule, and what must be documented?
questions.answer: The cure is $7,600; the forbearance collects $9,200 and leaves $13,100, which takes six more weeks at the restored $2,450 with a smaller final payment, extending the schedule from 9.10 weeks to fourteen. The review record, the cause of the shortfall, the revised amounts, the end date and the consequence of a missed payment all belong in writing.
questions.distractor: The cure is $7,350; the forbearance collects $9,200 and leaves $13,100, which is 5.35 weeks, so five more payments of $2,450 close the file with no final adjustment.
questions.correction: The recorded fee belongs in the cure figure, and partial weeks cannot be collected, so the schedule rounds up to six payments with a smaller final amount. Stating the extension in weeks, with the review evidence, is what makes the accommodation defensible rather than informal.

questions.prompt: A broker can place $80,000 at three percent commission on a transaction with a dollar cost of $28,000, or $45,000 at one and a half percent with a dollar cost of $9,000. Compensation is $2,400 against $675. What must the recommendation contain?
questions.answer: Both options priced in dollars and dates, the compensation on each stated explicitly, the needs analysis that identifies which amount is required, the option recommended and why, and the conditions that would change it.
questions.distractor: The compensation difference is a private commercial matter, so it need only be disclosed if the merchant asks which option pays the broker more.
questions.correction: Disclosure that arrives only on request is not disclosure. The SBA's conduct rules treat undisclosed relationships and dual compensation as good cause for sanctions, and the FTC's deception standard treats material omissions as deceptive, so the compensation on each option belongs in the recommendation before the merchant decides.

questions.prompt: A merchant is declined. What makes that decline defensible rather than a brush-off?
questions.answer: Specific principal reasons tied to the analysis, the arithmetic behind them, the conditions and evidence that would change the answer, a review date, and referral options such as free small-business advisers or a certified development company.
questions.distractor: A statement that the file does not meet internal criteria at this time, with an invitation to reapply later, because internal standards are the funder's own commercial judgement and need not be explained.
questions.correction: Regulation B requires that reasons for adverse action be specific and states that citing internal standards, policies or a qualifying-score failure is insufficient for creditors within its scope; the same specificity principle is the professional standard outside it. Reasons tied to numbers give the merchant something to act on; policy language gives them nothing.

questions.prompt: A merchant applies for $95,000. The file has four of twelve months of bank statements, a UCC search showing no entity filing but one filing under an owner's personal name, a processor report covering the same four months showing receipts of $61,400, and no business tax return. The merchant says the year was worth about $400,000 and that a prior advance was paid off. Walk through the sequence that turns this into a defensible recommendation.
questions.answer: Write the claim ledger: four documented months, eight absent, a personal-name filing unresolved, no tax return, no payoff document. Normalise the four months of receipts to about $15,350 a week and size against that rather than the asserted year, noting that the four months exclude the seasonal peak. State the verification plan: eight missing statement months, the tax return or transcripts, a payoff letter from the prior funder and a fresh search covering the owner's personal name. Recommend a conditional counter-offer sized to the evidence, with concentration and seasonality checks requested because neither can be assessed on four months.
questions.distractor: Treat the $400,000 assertion as the operating figure because the merchant has operated for years, note the personal filing as an owner matter outside the business, and recommend the requested amount subject to receiving the tax return.
questions.correction: Assertions are not evidence, and four months cannot establish a year or a season. The unresolved personal filing affects priority and the guarantee discussion, so it cannot be set aside. The defensible path is to size to the deposited evidence, name every missing item with its source, and set the conditions for a larger amount rather than assuming the merchant's figure is close enough.

questions.prompt: Two files both fail. File one fails because the requested amount exceeds what the trough can carry; file two fails because two of the five items needed to assess collateral cannot be produced. How should each refusal be written?
questions.answer: File one gets the arithmetic: the requested remittance against the trough month, the largest remittance that meets the stated coverage, and the conditions under which the larger amount would be revisited. File two gets the document list: exactly which items are missing, who can produce them, and confirmation that the answer would be reconsidered on receipt, with an interim size stated if one is supportable.
questions.distractor: Both get the same note, stating that the file does not currently meet criteria and inviting a new application in ninety days, since explaining the reasons might invite disputes about the analysis.
questions.correction: A reason that names a measurement or a document is checkable and actionable; a restatement of policy is neither. Regulation B requires specific reasons for creditors within its scope and rejects citations to internal standards, and that specificity principle is the professional standard outside it. Withholding the reasons also pushes the merchant toward a less careful funder with the same file, which is the outcome an honest refusal is meant to avoid.

questions.prompt: A merchant's twelve weeks show $198,000 of deposits including $22,000 of owner transfers and $14,000 of insurance proceeds. Existing debits are $2,200 a week and the funder proposes $1,900 a week. Separately, the merchant is six weeks into an obligation with $15,600 remaining out of a $52,000 total, and asks for a renewal offering $36,400 of new proceeds with a $68,640 total. Combine both analyses into one recommendation.
questions.answer: Normalised deposits are $162,000, or $13,500 a week; existing and proposed obligations total $4,100, which is 30.37 percent of normalised deposits. On the renewal, finishing the remaining $15,600 and taking a fresh $30,000 at a factor of 1.32 gives $55,200 of total payments against $68,640 on the renewal, a difference of $13,440 or 24.35 percent. Recommend against the renewal unless the money is needed in the next six weeks, and size any new obligation to the normalised deposit figure rather than the gross.
questions.distractor: Normalised deposits are $198,000, or $16,500 a week, so obligations are 24.85 percent; the renewal is acceptable because the new weekly payment is lower per remaining week than the current one.
questions.correction: Gross deposits include non-operating credits, so the ratios must be computed on $162,000. Weekly payment size is not a comparison basis; the totals to the end of each schedule are, and the renewal collects $13,440 more from the account for the same need. Both corrections follow from running the analysis before the offer rather than after.

questions.prompt: A merchant's receipts run from $38,000 in the weakest month to $72,000 in the strongest, averaging $54,791.67, and the funder proposes a fixed $5,600 weekly schedule. The merchant is also told the structure is percentage-based with a true-up. What should the recommendation say?
questions.answer: The fixed schedule equals $24,266.67 a month, which is 63.86 percent of the weakest month and 33.70 percent of the strongest, and it exceeds 45 percent of receipts in six of twelve months, so the structure does not match the season. If a percentage structure is claimed, the recommendation must specify the records that establish actual receipts, the interval for reconciliation, who computes it, how the difference is credited, and what happens if two periods pass without one; otherwise it should be treated and sized as a fixed debit.
questions.distractor: The schedule is 44.29 percent of average monthly receipts, which is acceptable, and the percentage description can be relied on because the funder names the structure in the agreement.
questions.correction: An average is not a period, and a structure's name is not its mechanics. The count of tight months is the finding that changes the recommendation, and a true-up without documented mechanics leaves the seasonal risk with the merchant, which is why the FTC's staff perspective flags providers that promise reconciliations and do not perform them.

questions.prompt: A merchant has $980,000 of revenue, $220,000 of eligible receivables, one customer representing $607,600 of revenue and $136,400 of receivables, a 25 percent single-obligor limit with an 80 percent advance rate, and 96 percent of receipts through one processor. The merchant wants $176,000 and needs $70,000 for inventory over six months plus $50,000.37 for a seven-year machine. What is the recommendation?
questions.answer: Availability is $110,880 with the limit applied, not $176,000, so the requested amount is unsupportable on the receivable base. The needs analysis separates $70,000 of six-month working capital from a $50,000.37 seven-year asset, which should be matched to different terms, and the processor dependency calls for a second processor, a notice obligation or a reserve of at least a week of receipts. Recommend the matched structure at the supported size, not the requested amount.
questions.distractor: Availability is $138,600 because the concentration limit reduces the eligible base by the customer's excess, and the requested amount can be supported by adding the equipment as additional collateral.
questions.correction: The limit acts before the advance rate, so the base falls to $138,600 and availability to $110,880. Naming the machine as collateral does not create revenue to service the obligation, and matching it to a seven-year term addresses the fit question that the request ignores. Both corrections come from doing the base arithmetic and the needs analysis before the sizing conversation.

questions.prompt: A merchant's guarantee is unlimited and joint and several between two owners, the agreement contains a springing dominion right at fifteen percent availability, and the broker is paid by the funder at a rate that is higher on the larger option. What must the merchant be told before signing?
questions.answer: That either owner can be pursued for the full remaining balance and that the split between them is a separate matter; that availability of $110,880 makes the fifteen percent threshold $16,632, with the notice period, cure route and effect on working cash explained; and that the broker is paid by the funder at a stated rate on each option, including what the smaller option pays.
questions.distractor: That the guarantee is shared equally between the two owners because both signed, that the availability threshold is a technical covenant that will not be exercised while payments are current, and that the broker's compensation is confidential commercial information.
questions.correction: Each of the three statements is wrong in a way that costs the merchant later: joint and several does not allocate the claim, control of collections can be triggered by a measured threshold without a missed payment, and compensation from the funder is precisely the fact that must be disclosed. The correction is to translate each clause into its number and its consequence in writing.

questions.prompt: A merchant is $7,600 behind, $22,300 remains, and collateral with an appraised orderly liquidation value of $31,000 is realised by a quick sale for $18,000. The guarantor asks what the funder can now claim. Walk through the position and the conduct requirements.
questions.answer: The $18,000 is applied to the balance, leaving a shortfall that can generally be claimed against the guarantor under the guarantee, subject to the documents and to law. The $13,000 gap between orderly liquidation value and the quick sale is the reason the commercially reasonable standard applies to every aspect of a disposition, including method, manner, time, place and price, so the funder should be able to show what was done and why; the guarantor should obtain legal advice about the shortfall.
questions.distractor: Realising the collateral discharges the obligation, so the funder can claim nothing further from the guarantor once the assets are sold, and the difference between appraisal and sale price is a loss the funder must absorb.
questions.correction: Proceeds reduce the balance rather than eliminating it, and a shortfall is normally enforceable against a guarantor unless the documents or the law provide otherwise. That is also why the commercially reasonable standard matters: a disposition that cannot be justified in method, marketing, timing and price is the kind of shortfall that ends up in a dispute rather than in a collection.

questions.prompt: A merchant holds three obligations: a daily card advance at $120 a day, an equipment loan at $610.42 a month and a weekly advance at $1,450. A consolidation is offered that leaves the equipment loan untouched. What must happen before the word consolidation is used?
questions.answer: List every obligation with its remaining balance and obtain a dated payoff letter for each one being retired, repay each, confirm what happens to the related filings, and compute total dollars and dates before and after. If the equipment loan remains in place, the transaction is a new obligation alongside it, and it must be described and priced that way.
questions.distractor: Describe it as a consolidation because it replaces two of the three obligations and simplifies the payment calendar, with the equipment loan excluded since it is secured on a specific asset.
questions.correction: The label describes an outcome, and the outcome here is a new obligation added to an existing one. Excluding a secured obligation can be legitimate, but only if the merchant is told that the total debt service is unchanged in that respect and sees both totals. Payoff letters and a before-and-after ledger are what make the description verifiable.

questions.prompt: A merchant has $21,400 of normalised weekly receipts, a 38 percent gross margin, $2,100 of existing weekly obligations, $2,900 of weekly fixed cost, a trough-to-peak ratio of 0.53 and one customer at 62 percent of revenue. The request is a $2,450 weekly remittance. Write the decision with its conditions.
questions.answer: Contribution is $8,132 and obligations plus fixed cost would be $7,450, giving coverage of 1.09, which is thin before tax, before the trough and before the concentration finding. Recommend a counter-offer of $1,900 a week for 1.18 coverage with total debt service at 18.69 percent of receipts; the largest remittance reaching 1.15 coverage is $2,071.30. Decline the requested amount today with reasons, and set conditions: eight weeks of statements showing contribution of at least $9,000 a week, the largest customer below 40 percent, no returned items in sixty days, and a second processor in place.
questions.distractor: Coverage of 1.09 is above one, so fund the requested amount and note the concentration and season as monitoring items to be reviewed at the next scheduled check-in.
questions.correction: Coverage above one is a starting position, not a conclusion, and monitoring items that require no action are not conditions. The correction is to give the merchant a number that works today, the single measurement that controls a larger amount, and a date for review, so the refusal has a route attached to it.

questions.prompt: A merchant shows $310,000 of six-month deposits including $45,000 from a new lender, $19,000 of owner transfers and $8,000 of tax refunds, with existing debits of $3,100 a week and seven returned items. The requested remittance is $2,300 a week. What does the analysis support, and what must still be checked?
questions.answer: Normalised deposits are $238,000 for the window, or about $9,153.85 a week if the window is twenty-six weeks, and existing plus requested obligations are $5,400, which is close to 59 percent of that weekly figure; the file needs the returned items explained and the timing of the existing debits before any commitment.
questions.distractor: Normalised deposits are $310,000, giving roughly $11,923.08 a week, so the $5,400 of obligations is about 45 percent of receipts and the returned items are a minor administrative matter.
questions.correction: Non-operating credits must be removed before any ratio, and the lender proceeds in particular will not recur. Obligations at roughly 59 percent of normalised weekly receipts leave little for cost of sales and fixed expenses, and seven returned items show how little slack the account has when a debit lands early. Both corrections must be applied before a sizing recommendation is offered.

questions.prompt: A filing taken on 2026-03-01 secures an advance, a renewal is proposed that pays off the outstanding balance in full, and an owner holds a separate filing recorded under their personal name against business assets. What does the analysis need to record?
questions.answer: That the filing taken on 2026-03-01 remains effective for five years to 2031-03-01, with continuation available only within the six months before expiration from 2030-09-01; that paying off the balance does not by itself terminate a financing statement, so a termination or amendment should be obtained and confirmed; and that a filing under a personal name must be read on its own terms because it will not appear in a search of the entity name, affecting both priority and the guarantee discussion.
questions.distractor: That the renewal automatically terminates the earlier filing because the underlying obligation is satisfied, and that the personal filing is irrelevant to the business's assets since it names an individual rather than the company.
questions.correction: Filing status depends on the record, not on the balance: effectiveness runs for five years subject to continuation within the six months before expiration, and a satisfied obligation can leave a live record. A filing naming an individual also needs separate treatment and a separate search, because a funder's own search is run against the name it is asked to search. Record each finding with its date and source.

questions.prompt: An advisor's note states that the recommended facility offers the fastest approval available, that the merchant should sign before a promised rate change, and that the commission structure need not be disclosed because the merchant did not ask. The merchant's need is $45,000 with a $9,000 dollar cost, and the alternative of $80,000 carries $28,000 of cost and pays the advisor $1,725 more. Rewrite the substance of the note.
questions.answer: Remove the unsupported speed claim and the manufactured deadline, disclose that the advisor is paid by the funder, one and a half percent on $45,000 and three percent on $80,000, and state the needs analysis that supports $45,000 at $54,000 of total repayment and $2,700 a week against the $80,000 option at $108,000 of total repayment and $4,153.85 a week. Record the conditions that would change the recommendation, such as a signed contract for the additional volume, and keep the note dated in the file.
questions.distractor: Keep the speed and deadline language as ordinary negotiation, disclose the commission only if the merchant asks directly, and recommend the $80,000 amount because a larger facility gives the merchant more room to grow.
questions.correction: Unsubstantiated claims and manufactured urgency are exactly the conduct the FTC's advertising guidance addresses, and an omission of compensation is material to the decision. More capital at a higher total cost is a different facility, not a better one, so the recommendation should follow the needs analysis, and the note should say which option was recommended and why even when the merchant chooses otherwise.
